title: Login CSRF: a cross-site form POST to /api/auth/sign-in/email was claimed to bypass Better Auth's origin check because it carries no cookie
description: The candidate held that Better Auth validates the Origin header only when the incoming request already carries a cookie, so a cookie-less login request is unchecked; an attacker page auto-submitting an application/x-www-form-urlencoded form with the attacker's own credentials to https://<SITE_URL>/api/auth/sign-in/email would then be forwarded verbatim by the TanStack proxy, answered with Set-Cookie, and the victim would browse inside the attacker's account. The web-tier observations underlying it are accurate -- the proxy adds no origin binding, the sole request middleware only sets response headers, SameSite=Lax means the victim's own cookie is not attached -- but the claimed library behaviour, which is the entire root cause, is contradicted by the best evidence available locally.
claimed_root_cause: The auth proxy (src/routes/api/auth/$.ts) and the Start middleware add no request-origin binding of their own, so the only cross-site control on POST /api/auth/sign-in/email is Better Auth's origin check, which by library design is conditioned on the presence of a cookie; login CSRF is exactly the cookie-less case.

trace.description: Any method and content type from any origin is accepted by the route handler; it performs no Origin, Referer or Sec-Fetch-Site inspection of its own.
Headers -- including a form content-type and the absence of any cookie -- and the raw body are copied verbatim into the upstream request handed to ba.handler (32).
sameSite 'lax' means the victim's existing interw.* cookies are not attached to a cross-site POST, so the request would reach Better Auth cookie-less -- the premise the candidate builds on.
Claimed sink: sign-in/email with the attacker's verified credentials succeeds and the response Set-Cookie installs the attacker's session in the victim's browser.

evidence.description: Vendored official Better Auth security skill (better-auth/skills, pinned at 20c9e88 in skills-lock.json and hash-guarded in CI): 'Multi-layer protection: origin header validation, Fetch Metadata checks, and first-login protection.' Fetch Metadata (Sec-Fetch-Site) does not depend on a cookie being present, and 'first-login protection' names precisely the cookie-less login case the candidate assumes is unguarded.

The whole `advanced` block is useSecureCookies, cookiePrefix and defaultCookieAttributes; a repo-wide grep finds no disableCSRFCheck and no disableOriginCheck anywhere, so Better Auth's default multi-layer CSRF protection is left enabled.
The same vendored skill set lists disableCSRFCheck and disableOriginCheck (124) as the options that would switch those layers off, each flagged as a security risk -- neither is set in this project.
trustedOrigins is [SITE_URL] and baseURL is the same origin, so an attacker page's Origin is outside the trusted set wherever Better Auth evaluates it.

The only request middleware registered is securityHeadersMiddleware, which sets response headers; this is accurate, but it means the web tier neither adds nor removes a cross-site control -- the verdict turns entirely on the library.
form-action 'self' restricts forms rendered by this origin, not an attacker page's form targeting it -- accurate, and not a control this candidate could have relied on either way.

reason: The candidate's root cause is a single library claim -- that Better Auth's origin validation runs only when the request already carries a cookie -- and that claim is refuted by evidence available locally, without installing anything. The official Better Auth security skill vendored into this repository (.agents/skills/better-auth-security-best-practices/SKILL.md:93, pinned to better-auth/skills@20c9e88 in skills-lock.json and re-hashed by the CI job skills-verify) states the CSRF protection is multi-layer: origin header validation, Fetch Metadata checks, and first-login protection. Two of those three are cookie-independent by construction, and 'first-login protection' is the vendor's name for exactly the scenario the candidate calls unprotected. The project leaves that protection at its default: a repo-wide grep finds no disableCSRFCheck and no disableOriginCheck, the `advanced` block (convex/auth.ts:76-84) sets only cookie attributes, and trustedOrigins is pinned to [SITE_URL] (49). The candidate's second, independent premise is equally unestablished and cuts the same way: a cross-site HTML form can only send application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain, and nothing shows better-call parses those into ctx.body for a JSON-declared endpoint rather than rejecting them -- if it rejects them there is no cross-site request shape at all. The remaining blockers (proxy forwarding, browser cookie storage) only matter downstream of a premise that local evidence contradicts. The supporting web-tier observations are correct and were re-verified -- src/routes/api/auth/$.ts:16-32 forwards method, headers and body verbatim with no Origin/Referer/Sec-Fetch-Site check, src/start.ts registers only a response-header middleware, and CSP form-action 'self' governs only forms on our own pages -- but they describe the absence of a redundant control, not a defeated one, and no unauthorized identity, state or disclosure follows from them. Adding an explicit Sec-Fetch-Site check in the proxy would be defence in depth, not a fix for a demonstrated boundary violation. Rejected rather than parked as needs_validation because the decisive fact was answerable from repository content, and it answers against the candidate.

title: Pre-hijack: an attacker-registered, unverified password account for the victim's address can become the victim's identity once any trusted method verifies that address
description: Signup is open and unauthenticated: anyone can POST /api/auth/sign-up/email (proxied verbatim at src/routes/api/auth/$.ts:29) with victim@example.com and a password of the attacker's choosing. Better Auth persists the user with emailVerified=false plus a credential account; requireEmailVerification (convex/auth.ts:105) blocks the attacker's sign-in but nothing in this repository ever removes, rejects or even reads that unverified credential account -- `emailVerified` is written in exactly one place (convex/auth.ts:209) and read nowhere. When the real owner arrives, typically through an org invitation, invitations.preview reports accountExists=true (convex/invitations.ts:124) and /accept-invite therefore renders SignInToAccept (src/routes/accept-invite.$token.tsx:143), which offers only a password field the victim does not know and a magic-link button; no fresh sign-up path exists on that card. If the magic-link plugin (disableSignUp, convex/auth.ts:298) resolves the attacker-created user, opens a session on it and marks it verified, provisionAppUser (convex/lib/auth.ts:49) binds the Convex users row to that BA user and invitations.accept inserts the org membership on it (convex/invitations.ts:179); the attacker then signs in with the address and the password they chose and holds the victim's Convex identity and org memberships. A second completion needs no magic link at all: sendOnSignUp (convex/auth.ts:139) already mails the victim a 'Verify your email ... You'll be signed in automatically' link (convex/emailTemplates.ts:312-313) whose footer says 'If you didn't create an account, you can safely ignore this email', and per the vendored official Better Auth skill the same mail is re-sent on every unverified sign-in attempt, so the attacker can re-deliver it on demand within the verificationSend bucket; one victim click flips the flag on the attacker's account. With Google enabled, accountLinking.enabled without trustedProviders (convex/auth.ts:178-182) is the OAuth variant of the same merge. What remains unproven offline is whether Better Auth actually performs any of those three transitions on a user whose emailVerified is false.
claimed_root_cause: convex/auth.ts enables three ways to prove an address (password + verification mail, magic link, optional Google) but treats the unverified password account an arbitrary caller created as the same identity a later mailbox-proving method lands on. The invariant the repository documents at KNOWN_ISSUES.md:59 -- 'the attacker's password account stays unverified, so BA refuses to link it' -- holds only if every trusted method refuses to sign into, verify or link into an existing unverified user; no hook in this repository (databaseHooks.user.create.before, user.update.after, sendMagicLink) enforces that, and provisionAppUser's email fallback (convex/lib/auth.ts:56-65) explicitly assumes every BA user email is verified and unique.

trace.description: Password sign-up is enabled for any address with no invitation or allow-list gate; the BA user and its credential account are created by whoever submits the form, reachable unauthenticated through the proxy at src/routes/api/auth/$.ts:29.
requireEmailVerification blocks the attacker's own sign-in but leaves the user row and credential account in place; this is the single control the whole chain has to defeat.
The victim is mailed a generic 'Verify your email' link at the moment the attacker registers their address (convex/emailTemplates.ts:310-321).
Clicking that link is advertised to sign the clicker in automatically -- into the attacker-created user, since that is the only user holding the address.

disableSignUp restricts magic links to users that already exist -- the attacker-created user qualifies; sendMagicLink (299-315) mails the address without inspecting emailVerified or the presence of a foreign credential account.
accountExists is computed from the Better Auth user table by email (119-123) and is true for the attacker-created user.

accountExists routes the invitee to SignInToAccept (239-373): a read-only email field, a password the victim does not know (325-350) and a magic-link button (358-367) wired to authClient.signIn.magicLink (274-286). No sign-up branch is offered once an account exists.

Whatever BA session the victim ends up with resolves to the attacker-created BA id; the Convex users row is created for it, or an existing row is re-pointed to it through the by_email fallback (56-65).
organizationMembers is inserted for that shared user after the email-match check passes (175-177) -- the addresses do match, because both principals are the same BA user.
Once emailVerified is true on that user, sign-in/email with the address and the attacker's chosen password is accepted and the session carries the victim's Convex identity, org memberships and role.

evidence.description: The only write of emailVerified in the entire repository (token-gated invite pre-verification). A repo-wide grep for `emailVerified` returns this line and the comment above it and nothing else: no code path removes, flags or refuses an unverified credential account, and nothing reads the flag before linking or provisioning.

'Verified email closes the hole : the attacker's password account stays unverified, so BA refuses to link it.' The repository's stated threat model (53-60 describes exactly this attacker) rests entirely on a Better Auth behaviour it never verifies in code.
accountLinking.enabled with no trustedProviders: the Google variant of the merge, where a verified Google identity for the same address would link into the existing unverified user.

The verification mail tells the recipient 'If you didn't create an account, you can safely ignore this email' while line 312 promises 'You'll be signed in automatically' -- a victim who did not register has no signal that the account is foreign and clicking is the advertised action.

Vendored official Better Auth skill (pinned in skills-lock.json to better-auth/skills@20c9e88): with requireEmailVerification enabled, 'unverified users will receive a new verification email on each sign-in attempt'. The attacker can therefore re-deliver the verification mail to the victim at will, without the victim ever touching a magic link.
verificationSend bounds those mails per recipient address (capacity 3, 5/h) but bounds nothing about the single click that completes the takeover.
The product's own sign-up surface is unauthenticated and takes an arbitrary email; nothing upstream of Better Auth restricts which address may be registered.

blockers: better-auth@1.6.30 is not installed (node_modules absent, installation prohibited): whether the magic-link verify handler signs a session for an existing user whose emailVerified is false -- and whether it sets emailVerified=true on that user -- must be read from node_modules/better-auth/dist/plugins/magic-link. If it refuses unverified users the primary chain dies at the invite card; if it verifies them the takeover completes with no victim action beyond using the invitation.

Whether GET /verify-email sets emailVerified=true on an existing unverified user and, with autoSignInAfterVerification, opens a session on it (node_modules/better-auth/dist/api/routes/verify-email). This is the second, magic-link-free completion: the mail is already sent at sign-up and re-sent on each of the attacker's sign-in attempts, so only this transition is unproven.

For the Google variant: whether handleOAuthUserInfo links a verified provider identity into an existing user whose emailVerified is false when accountLinking.enabled is set with no trustedProviders, and whether it updates that user's emailVerified on link (node_modules/better-auth/dist/oauth2/link-account).

validation_plan.local: In a disposable checkout that already has node_modules (offline, never this sandbox, no install here): (a) read the three library files named in the blockers for the decisive branches. (b) Then a vitest, entirely in-process against a memory adapter and dummy @test.local addresses, with betterAuth({ database: memoryAdapter(), emailAndPassword: { enabled: true, requireEmailVerification: true, minPasswordLength: 12 }, emailVerification: { sendOnSignUp: true, autoSignInAfterVerification: true, sendVerificationEmail: capture }, account: { accountLinking: { enabled: true } }, plugins: [magicLink({ disableSignUp: true, sendMagicLink: capture })] }): step 1 signUp.email('victim@test.local', 'attacker-password-12'); assert user.emailVerified === false and a credential account exists. Step 2 signIn.magicLink('victim@test.local'), GET the captured URL, then assert whether a session was issued and whether the stored user's emailVerified became true -- and that the user id is the one created in step 1. Step 3 signIn.email('victim@test.local', 'attacker-password-12') and record whether it returns a session for that same user id. Step 4 repeats steps 2-3 using instead the verification URL captured from sendOnSignUp (and the one re-sent by a failed step-3 sign-in) to cover the magic-link-free completion. No network, no mail delivery, no deployment involved.
validation_plan.deployment: On a non-production deployment only, with two mailboxes the owner controls and no third-party address: from browser profile A register mailbox B's address with a password P; check the Better Auth user and account rows for that address (emailVerified, provider list) in the Convex dashboard. Invite B to a throwaway organisation; from browser profile B open the invite link, record whether the card offers sign-in only, use the magic-link button, accept, then re-read the same rows. Finally, from profile A sign in with B's address and P and record whether /app opens B's organisation. Do not run this against production, and delete the throwaway org and both users afterwards.

title: POST /api/chat skips the per-user chatSend rate limiter that every other chat-generation path enforces, giving any org member unmetered paid model calls and unbounded agent-thread creation
description: The Convex site origin registers POST /api/chat unconditionally (convex/http.ts:28-32), handled by chat.streamOverHttp (convex/chat.ts:274-311). Both in-app generation paths charge the caller's per-user token bucket 'chatSend' before doing any paid work: sendMessage at convex/chat.ts:168 and respondToToolApproval at convex/chat.ts:213, both via consumeLimit (convex/rateLimiters.ts:70-83) against the bucket declared at convex/rateLimiters.ts:31-32 with the comment 'Chat messages: per user. AI calls are expensive.'. streamOverHttp resolves the bearer identity (chat.ts:275), validates org membership through internal.chat.actionAuthProbe -> requireOrgMember (chat.ts:287-289, convex/lib/auth.ts:107-120), then goes straight to chatAgent.streamText (chat.ts:300-304). It never calls consumeLimit, creates a brand-new durable agent thread on every request that omits threadId (chat.ts:292-294), and imposes no cap on body.prompt (chat.ts:303). A verified account that is a member of any organisation -- including one it created itself through the unmetered organizations.create (convex/organizations.ts:74-105) -- can therefore drive as many Anthropic generations as it likes, each worth up to ten model steps (convex/agent.ts:23), and persist one new thread per request, entirely outside the budget the operator set for exactly this action. The route is dead code as far as the product is concerned: no file under src/ references it.
root_cause: streamOverHttp (convex/chat.ts:274-311) was added as a second door onto the same paid action as sendMessage but reproduces only the authentication and authorization half of that handler. It omits the consumeLimit(ctx, 'chatSend', user._id) call that sendMessage (chat.ts:168) and respondToToolApproval (chat.ts:213) perform, and it creates a thread per request with no cap, so the chatSend bucket is enforced on the mutation paths only and not on the HTTP entry that reaches the same agent.
intended_behavior: Every chat generation, whichever entry point triggers it, is charged to the caller's per-user chatSend bucket ('Chat messages: per user. AI calls are expensive.', convex/rateLimiters.ts:31), so a single user cannot exceed 30 generations per minute (burst 10) nor accumulate unbounded agent threads and messages.

trace.description: Public POST route on the Convex site origin, registered unconditionally, whose handler is chat.streamOverHttp. No client code under src/ calls it; it is reachable purely because it is registered.
authComponent.safeGetAuthUser(ctx) resolves the identity a Convex httpAction takes from the Authorization bearer JWT; a caller with no identity is answered 401 at line 276 and reaches nothing.

ctx.runQuery(internal.chat.actionAuthProbe, { orgId }) runs requireOrgMember on the body-supplied orgId (convex/lib/auth.ts:107-120); a non-member throws ConvexError('not_a_member'). This is the last check performed before the paid call when the body carries no threadId, and no consumeLimit follows it anywhere in the handler.
createThread(ctx, components.agent, { userId: scope }) runs on every request whose body omits threadId, creating one new durable agent thread per call with no cap, quota or cleanup.

chatAgent.streamText issues the paid Anthropic generation (up to stepCountIs(10) steps with the read-only recruiter tools, convex/agent.ts:23) on a prompt of unbounded length (line 303), having never consulted the chatSend bucket.

evidence.description: sendMessage: `await consumeLimit(ctx, 'chatSend', user._id)` immediately after requireOrgMember and before saving the prompt or scheduling streamAsync -- the intended per-user budget on this exact action.
respondToToolApproval also consumes chatSend before resuming generation. streamOverHttp (274-311) is the only generation path in the file that contains no consumeLimit call.

`chatSend: { kind: 'token bucket', rate: 30, period: MINUTE, capacity: 10 }` keyed per user -- the operator's declared bound, annotated at line 31 as 'Chat messages: per user. AI calls are expensive.'
`{ prompt: body.prompt }` -- the raw JSON body field is forwarded to streamText with no length validation; body is a bare cast (chat.ts:278-282), not a validator.
`stopWhen: stepCountIs(10)` -- a single streamText call is worth up to ten model steps plus the tool queries they make, so each unmetered request is a multiple of one generation.

organizations.create requires only requireAppUser and inserts an organizationMembers row with role 'owner' for the caller, so any registered user can satisfy the membership precondition with an org of their own; the mutation itself consumes no limiter.
The /api/chat route is registered with no access comment and no wrapper, unlike /resend-webhook at lines 18-26 which carries an explicit `// access:` justification.

conditions.description: Caller holds a valid Convex bearer JWT for a Better Auth account. Signup is self-service: email+password with requireEmailVerification (convex/auth.ts:103-105), plus invitation and optional Google.

Caller is a member of any role of the organisation named in the request body. Any registered user can satisfy this by creating their own organisation, which makes them its owner (convex/organizations.ts:74-105).
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is configured on the Convex deployment so chatAgent.streamText reaches the provider; the route is registered unconditionally in convex/http.ts, with no feature flag.

The only remaining bounds are outside the repository: Convex per-deployment HTTP-action concurrency and body limits, and the Anthropic account's rate and spend limits. These throttle the deployment as a whole rather than the abusing user, so when they bite they degrade chat for every tenant.

execution.attacker_perspective: An authenticated member of any organisation, including one it created for itself moments earlier, sends repeated JSON POSTs to https://<deployment>.convex.site/api/chat carrying the Convex bearer token the SPA already holds. Each request yields a new durable agent thread and a full agent generation, and none of them is counted against the chatSend bucket that caps the same action in the product UI.
payloads: POST /api/chat  Authorization: Bearer <convex-jwt>  Content-Type: application/json  {"orgId":"<an org the caller belongs to>","prompt":"prompt 0"}
the same request repeated N times with no threadId field (verifier harness used N=5) -- each one creates a thread and a paid model call
{"orgId":"<own org id>","prompt":"<307200-byte string>"} -- accepted, forwarded to the model with no app-level prompt cap
instructions: Bounded local check only; no deployment, network or external service was contacted (the sandbox has no network interfaces).

The verifier wrote its own loader hook and stubs rather than reusing the hunter's, in /root/security-audit-skill/interw/run-1/agents/verifier-v04/scratch/h/ : hooks.mjs maps the absent packages convex/values, convex/server, @convex-dev/agent and @convex-dev/rate-limiter, and the identity/paid/mail modules ./agent, ./auth, ../email, ../emailTemplates, to in-memory recorders; convex/chat.ts, convex/rateLimiters.ts, convex/lib/auth.ts, convex/lib/instructions.ts and convex/_generated/{api,server}.js load unmodified from the read-only repo.

Run: /root/security-audit-skill/interw/run-1/parent-tools/sandbox.sh verifier-v04 'cd h && node --experimental-strip-types --import ./register.mjs ./verify-chat.mjs'. Full output retained at scratch-relative chat-verify.log (promote if needed as evidence for the observed result below).

Fixture: users_A owner of org_A, users_B owner of org_B; identity switched through the ./auth stub; ctx.runQuery dispatches internal.chat.actionAuthProbe to the real handler after a v.id('organizations')-style argument check.
Case 2 (the claim): identity users_A, five invocations of chat.streamOverHttp with {orgId:'org_A', prompt:'p<i>'} and no threadId; record limiter calls, createThread calls and paid model calls.
Cases 3 and 3b (positive controls): invoke chat.sendMessage.handler and chat.respondToToolApproval.handler as the same user on one of those threads and record limiter calls.

Cases 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 (bounding the claim): anonymous, non-member org, foreign-scope threadId, 300 KiB prompt, malformed JSON, missing prompt -- to establish that authentication, membership and thread scoping are intact and that only the limiter and the prompt cap are missing.
execution.observed_result: Case 1 anonymous: 401, 0 threads, 0 model calls. Case 2: five 200 responses with X-Thread-Id thread_1..thread_5; limiterCalls 0, threadsCreated 5, paidModelCalls 5, each agent call logged as createThread + PAID_MODEL_CALL under scope 'org_A:users_A'. Case 3 control: sendMessage on thread_1 recorded limiterCalls [{name:'chatSend', key:'users_A'}] and scheduled chat:streamAsync. Case 3b control: respondToToolApproval recorded the same chatSend consumption. Case 4 non-member: ConvexError not_a_member with 0 threads and 0 model calls. Case 5 foreign-scope threadId: ConvexError forbidden with 0 model calls. Case 6: 200 with the model call receiving promptBytes 307200 and 0 limiter calls. Case 7 malformed JSON: SyntaxError thrown after authentication, nothing reached. Case 8 missing prompt: 400, nothing reached. Total limiter calls recorded across every streamOverHttp invocation in the run: 0. This independently reproduces the hunter's result: membership and thread-scope enforcement hold, the per-user budget does not.

remediation.strategy: Preferred: delete the route -- nothing under src/ calls it, and the in-app path (sendMessage + listMessages) already covers the product. If it must stay, make it pay the same budget as the mutation paths rather than trusting a second door: turn actionAuthProbe into an internalMutation that performs requireOrgMember and consumeLimit('chatSend', user._id) as one unit and is called with ctx.runMutation, so the limiter is structurally inseparable from the membership check instead of being a call someone can forget again; additionally validate the body (it is currently a bare cast, chat.ts:278-282), cap prompt length, and require an existing threadId rather than minting a durable thread per request. Regression test: load convex/chat.ts with @convex-dev/rate-limiter and @convex-dev/agent mocked and assert that streamOverHttp records a limit('chatSend', <userId>) call before any streamText call, mirroring the assertion for sendMessage -- the harness in this verification is a working template for it. Note for the reviewer: fixing this does not remove the need for a bound on organizations.create, which is itself unmetered and is what makes the membership precondition free to satisfy.

likelihood.reason: The prerequisites are cheap and entirely self-service: a verified email+password account (convex/auth.ts:103-105), an organisation the caller creates for itself in one unmetered mutation (convex/organizations.ts:74-105), and the bearer token the SPA already holds. The route sits on the public .convex.site origin at a conventional path and is registered unconditionally. It is not, however, exercised by any client code, so an attacker has to look for it rather than stumble on it; the repository's own prior review already recorded the same gap (docs/audit/2026-09-15/pipeline-ia-stockage.md:772-782), which corroborates that it is a real and findable surface.

impact.reason: An explicit security control is fully defeated on this path -- locally observed as five paid model calls against zero limiter consumptions, versus one consumption on the control path -- but what it protects is operator cost and shared capacity, not data or privilege. Each unmetered request is worth up to ten model steps (convex/agent.ts:23) on an unbounded prompt and leaves one new durable agent thread with its messages behind. The blast radius reaches other tenants only indirectly, when the shared Anthropic key or the deployment's action concurrency throttles. Authentication, org membership and thread scoping all held under test, so there is no disclosure and no privilege gain.

confidence.reason: Every cited line was re-read at HEAD 9a70f3f (http.ts:28-32; chat.ts:168, 213, 274-311; rateLimiters.ts:31-32, 70-83; agent.ts:23; lib/auth.ts:107-120; organizations.ts:74-105), and the result was reproduced independently with the verifier's own stubs and loader, not the hunter's: 0 limiter calls across 5 paid model calls on the HTTP path against 1 limiter call on each of the two control paths, with the negative cases confirming that only the meter is missing. The residual unknowns are deployment-side (Convex concurrency and body limits, Anthropic tier) and none of them restores a per-user bound.

title: emailEvents.recent (and sessions.countsForOrg) are scoped by organisation only, handing every member the candidate addresses and session ids of restricted roles they are hidden from
description: Restricted projects are hidden from members not named on them: projects.list, getBySlug, sessions.listByProject, reports.forSession, reports.searchCandidates and dashboard.overview all apply canSeeProject or filterVisibleProjects and resolve to not_found, because 'a recruiter should not learn that a confidential role exists' (convex/lib/projectAccess.ts:7-10). The deliverability query emailEvents.recent is scoped only by organisation: it applies requireOrgMember and then returns, for up to 200 emailLog rows of the org, the recipient address, the template, the delivery status and the sessionId. sessions.sendInvitation writes exactly that — the candidate's address and their session id — for every invitation, including invitations to restricted projects. A plain member excluded from a confidential search can therefore read the addresses of every candidate invited to it, when they were invited and whether the mail bounced, plus the session ids. sessions.countsForOrg carries the same org-only scoping and lets the same member count the hidden sessions by differencing against dashboard.overview, which does filter. Both are public Convex queries reachable by any authenticated member; neither has a caller anywhere under src/, so no UI path is needed and none exists to notice the difference.
root_cause: emailLog rows carry orgId and sessionId but no project reference (convex/schema.ts:553-575), and emailEvents.recent (convex/emailEvents.ts:59-78) applies only requireOrgMember at line 62 before reading by_org_and_created at line 65 and returning recipient (line 71) and sessionId (line 74); sessions.countsForOrg (convex/sessions.ts:295-311) is scoped the same way at lines 298-303. The primary reads over the same underlying data (convex/dashboard.ts:30-44, convex/reports.ts:290-302) do apply the project-visibility predicate, so the derived reads disagree with the policy they are derived from.
intended_behavior: Every read that names, counts or dates a candidate of a restricted project should pass through the same visibility predicate as the primary reads. convex/reports.ts:288-289 states it for search ('otherwise a confidential role leaks through the search box'), convex/notifications.ts:79-80 states it for notification audiences ('who sees the role is who hears about it'), and convex/lib/projectAccess.ts:9-10 states the stronger form: an invisible project must resolve to not_found rather than be discoverable at all.

trace.description: A plain org member, excluded from a restricted project, calls the public query with their own orgId.
Only requireOrgMember(ctx, orgId) is applied; the returned member.role and the caller's projectShares are discarded.

Provenance of the rows being read: every invitation inserts an emailLog row with recipient = session.candidateEmail (line 224) and sessionId = session._id (line 227), whether or not the session's project is restricted.
The whole organisation's emailLog is read through by_org_and_created, newest first, up to 200 rows, with no per-row filtering.
recipient — the candidate's email address — is returned to the excluded member, alongside template, status, createdAt and, at line 74, the sessionId of the hidden session.

evidence.description: Stated policy: an invisible project resolves to not_found, not 'forbidden', because 'a recruiter should not learn that a confidential role exists'.
emailLog is defined with orgId, template, recipient, status, providerId, error, sessionId and createdAt — no projectId, so no index on this table can express project visibility.
The invitation emailLog row is written with recipient = the candidate's address (and sessionId at line 227).
The sessionId of the hidden session is returned alongside the recipient.
countsForOrg takes 500 sessions by the by_org index with no visibility filter, so its counts include sessions of projects the caller cannot see.

dashboard.overview filters its sessions to visibleProjectIds built by filterVisibleProjects (line 30): the primary read applies the policy the derived reads omit, and the difference between the two counts is the hidden-session count.

searchCandidates re-applies the restricted/projectShares check at retrieval time with the comment that otherwise 'a confidential role leaks through the search box' — the pattern emailEvents.recent lacks.
sendReportReady narrows its audience to the creator plus the named shares for a restricted project, confirming the intended policy for anything derived from a restricted role.
The prior hand-written review already lists emailEvents.recent as dead code with no interface; the public Convex function nonetheless remains deployed and callable.

conditions.description: Registered, authenticated user provisioned in the Convex users table.

Plain member of the organisation who is not named on the restricted project and is not its creator (admins and owners see everything by design). Cross-organisation reads are not possible: requireOrgMember rejects a foreign orgId with not_a_member, verified locally.

title: Transactional email templates interpolate the action URL raw into HTML; a caller-shaped Better Auth redirectTo/callbackURL would inject markup into first-party reset, verification and magic-link emails
description: convex/emailTemplates.ts escapes every user-supplied string with esc() but writes the `url` argument unescaped into href="${cta.url}" in layout() and as raw inner HTML in urlFallback(). For resetPasswordEmail, verificationEmail and magicLinkEmail (and, on the same layout, changeEmailVerificationEmail and deleteAccountVerificationEmail) that url is Better Auth's data.url, which BA assembles from the request's redirectTo / callbackURL. Independently reproduced locally against the real module: rendering the three templates with url = 'https://app.example/api/auth/reset-password/TOK?callbackURL=https://app.example/">Reactivate your accountx' passes isInternalPath and is returned verbatim) and login.tsx hands to authClient.sendVerificationEmail as callbackURL. The victim would receive a DKIM-authenticated first-party email whose HTML carries attacker-chosen links and text — phishing with the application's own sender reputation. What is not source-visible is the middle leg: whether better-auth 1.6.30 percent-encodes that parameter when building data.url, and whether its origin check tolerates '"', '<' and '>' in a same-origin or rooted value.
claimed_root_cause: layout() (convex/emailTemplates.ts:41) and urlFallback() (line 110) treat the `url` argument as safe HTML while the Better Auth senders in convex/auth.ts (lines 111-124, 141-154, 299-307) pass a URL that embeds a caller-supplied redirect parameter; trustedOrigins is an origin comparison, not a character filter, and the templates apply esc() to every other interpolated value but not to url.

trace.description: Anonymous POST to /api/auth/forgot-password (also /send-verification-email and /sign-in/magic-link) carrying a caller-chosen redirectTo / callbackURL in the body; the handler proxies method, headers and body unchanged to the Better Auth routes.

Better Auth invokes the sender with data.url assembled from that request. The only in-repo controls are trustedOrigins: [siteUrl] (line 49), the BA rule '/forgot-password': 3 per 60 s (line 62) and the per-email application limit consumed at line 116.
`url: data.url` is forwarded verbatim into resetPasswordEmail; the identical pattern reaches verificationEmail at line 154 and magicLinkEmail at line 307.
url is placed into the body paragraphs via urlFallback(locale, url) and into the call-to-action at line 394 (`cta: { label: c.cta, url }`), with no esc() applied to it at either site.

`<a href="${cta.url}"` — a url containing '"><a …>' closes the href attribute and injects arbitrary markup into the HTML body of the outgoing DKIM-signed email; urlFallback (line 112) additionally writes the same url as raw inner HTML inside a <span>.

evidence.description: esc() is defined here and applied to inviterName, orgName, candidateName, jobTitle, recommendation, newEmail, email and name in every HTML branch — re-verified locally by rendering invitationEmail with 'X' and '">', both of which come back entity-encoded — but it is never applied to `url`.
urlFallback interpolates ${url} as raw inner HTML inside a <span> in the English branch, and identically in the French branch on line 113.

verificationEmail passes url unescaped into cta; magicLinkEmail does the same at line 498, and changeEmailVerificationEmail (line 229) and deleteAccountVerificationEmail (line 294) share the same layout() sink with their own Better Auth data.url.
trustedOrigins: [siteUrl] is the only in-repo content control over redirectTo / callbackURL, and it is an origin comparison performed inside Better Auth rather than a character filter.
sendMagicLink forwards the Better Auth-built url to magicLinkEmail at line 307; disableSignUp: true on line 298 means the victim must already hold an account for the magic-link and reset variants.

The application itself hands the ?redirect= search param straight to authClient.sendVerificationEmail as callbackURL, so a crafted /login?redirect=… link is a second, first-party way for attacker characters to reach Better Auth's URL assembly.

internalRedirectSearch only .refine()s with isInternalPath; it does not normalise. Verified locally with the same probe-origin logic: '/">Sign in' is accepted (it starts with '/' and resolves to the probe origin) and the raw string — quotes and angle brackets intact — is what the route hands on.

better-auth is pinned at exactly 1.6.30, and no copy of that package exists anywhere on this machine (node_modules absent, the pnpm store holds only registry metadata), so its URL-assembly behaviour cannot be read.

blockers: better-auth@1.6.30 (pinned at pnpm-lock.yaml:2735) is not available offline — node_modules is absent, installation is prohibited, and the pnpm store under /root/.cache/pnpm contains only registry metadata — so it is not source-visible whether /forgot-password, /send-verification-email and /sign-in/magic-link percent-encode redirectTo / callbackURL when assembling data.url, nor whether the trustedOrigins / origin check rejects '"', '<' or '>' inside a same-origin absolute or rooted value.

Without Better Auth and its dependencies no bounded local run of the request-to-data.url leg is possible, so that leg of the trace could not be executed. Only the data.url-to-HTML leg was demonstrated, by loading convex/emailTemplates.ts (which has no imports at all) under node --experimental-strip-types inside the sandbox.

validation_plan.local: With dependencies installed offline, instantiate createAuth with sendResetPassword, sendVerificationEmail and sendMagicLink stubbed to capture data.url, and drive auth.handler directly (no deployed endpoint) with POST /forgot-password body {email:'victim@example.test', redirectTo:'/">x'} and with the absolute same-origin form 'https:///">x', then the analogous callbackURL for /send-verification-email and /sign-in/magic-link. If a captured url still contains the raw '">' sequence, feed it to resetPasswordEmail and assert the rendered html contains '' as a second anchor — that second step is already demonstrated and yields three anchors instead of one. If Better Auth encodes or rejects the value in every case, the candidate is disproved. Either outcome, apply esc() to cta.url, cta.label and the urlFallback url as defence in depth: the template must not depend on a library's encoding choices, and the one-line change is verifiable by the same local render.
validation_plan.deployment: On a non-production deployment with RESEND_TEST_MODE left at its default and the owner's own mailbox as the victim address, the owner sends the same forgot-password request from their own client and inspects the delivered email's HTML source (or the Resend dashboard's stored payload) for an anchor pointing outside SITE_URL after the reset button. No audit traffic is sent to production, and the only recipient is the owner.

title: files.setMyAvatar attaches any _storage id without binding it to the caller, so a plain member deletes the organisation logo — an admin-only asset — through the avatar path
description: files.setMyAvatar takes a storageId straight from the client and validates only that the blob exists, is at most 20 MB and has an allowed image content type; nothing checks that the caller uploaded it or that another row already owns it. The id is written to the caller's users.avatarStorageId, and the caller's next removeMyAvatar (or a second successful setMyAvatar) calls ctx.storage.delete on it. organizations.bySlug spreads the whole organisation row to every member, logoStorageId included, and every page under /app/$orgSlug loads that query, so a plain member already holds the logo's storage id. Calling setMyAvatar with it and then removeMyAvatar deletes the organisation's logo blob even though setOrgLogo and removeOrgLogo are admin-only; the organisation row keeps a dangling logoStorageId and resolveLogoUrl then returns null for every member on every page. The same primitive reaches any _storage id the caller learns — a colleague's avatar id would do — but the app's other queries expose only resolved avatarUrl values, so the organisation logo is the case reachable from data the member is given.
root_cause: convex/files.ts:40-54 (setMyAvatar) and 56-69 (removeMyAvatar), together with validateImage at convex/files.ts:16-30, treat a client-supplied Id<'_storage'> as owned by the caller: validateImage reads _storage metadata for any id (line 20) and never compares it to the caller, setMyAvatar stores it after requireAppUser only (lines 43-49), and the later delete (line 61, or line 46 on the next attach) runs on whatever id was stored. Convex file storage has no per-file owner — the _storage system table carries only _id, _creationTime, contentType, sha256 and size (convex/_generated/ai/guidelines.md file-storage section) — and convex/organizations.ts:126 puts the logo's id in every member's hands by spreading the organisations row.
intended_behavior: Only an organisation's admins or owner may change or remove its logo (convex/files.ts:74 and 91 both call requireOrgRole(ctx, orgId, 'admin')), and a user's avatar operations should be able to attach and delete only blobs that user attached themselves — never one that another users or organizations row references.

trace.description: The whole organisation row is spread to any member, logoStorageId included; every page under /app/$orgSlug calls this query (for example src/routes/app/$orgSlug/projects.$projectSlug.index.tsx:41), so the member already holds the raw storage id.
The member calls setMyAvatar with the logo's storage id; the only guard is requireAppUser — any registered user passes it.
The blob's _storage metadata is read for existence, size and content type; an organisation logo is an image under 20 MB, so it passes. Ownership is never considered.
The foreign id is written to the caller's own users.avatarStorageId, which is what makes it the caller's to delete.
ctx.storage.delete(user.avatarStorageId) runs on the organisation's logo blob; Convex storage has no per-file ownership to refuse it.

ctx.storage.getUrl(org.logoStorageId) now returns null and the organisation row still points at the deleted blob, so the logo is gone for every member on every page while only an admin was ever allowed to remove it.

evidence.description: setOrgLogo calls requireOrgRole(ctx, orgId, 'admin') — logo management is intended to be admin-only.
removeOrgLogo is likewise admin-only, and its body is the same ctx.storage.delete the avatar path reaches without a role check.
validateImage's only rejection for an unknown blob is not_found; for a blob that exists it checks size and contentType and returns, so any existing image id of the deployment is accepted.
A second successful setMyAvatar also deletes the previously stored id, so the primitive can be repeated without ever calling removeMyAvatar.
organizations.logoStorageId is a plain optional Id<'_storage'> field of the organisations row — the row bySlug spreads.

bySlug returns `...org`, so logoStorageId reaches every member's client; by contrast users.me (convex/users.ts:59) and organizations.listMembers (convex/organizations.ts:31) expose only a resolved avatarUrl, never an avatar storage id.

cascadeDelete calls ctx.storage.delete on a blob attached in an earlier session, and removeOrgLogo does the same for a logo uploaded by a different admin: the application itself depends on ctx.storage.delete accepting any id, which is why no ownership check exists to stop this one.

That is the documented API shape (the _storage system table carries no owner field) and the app's own admin flows depend on it, but the deletion itself was modelled by a fake ctx.storage in the local run, not observed against a live Convex deployment.

title: 300 MiB per-answer uploads reach a transcription action that buffers the whole object and a 5-slot pool shared by every tenant
description: A candidate holding a link may presign each answer up to MAX_SEGMENT_BYTES = 300 MiB: validateMedia accepts any positive integer content length up to that bound and requestSegmentUpload signs it into the PUT, so the browser can legitimately upload an object of that size per question. Nothing on the server ties an answer's byte size or duration to the recruiter's question.maxResponseSeconds, and markSegmentUploaded accepts whatever durationSeconds the client reports. After finish, onSessionCompleted enqueues transcribeSegment per uploaded answer; that action streams the object out of the bucket and materialises it entirely with new Response(stream).blob() before posting it to the provider with a 300 s timeout, in the default Convex runtime (convex/pipeline.ts carries no 'use node' — only convex/jobImportFetch.ts does). Failures are rethrown so the workpool retries, up to 4 attempts per segment, on mediaPool with maxParallelism 5, which the workpools comment notes is a deployment-wide ceiling shared by every organisation. Which of two outcomes follows is not decidable from the repository: if the runtime's action memory ceiling is below the buffered object the job fails on every attempt while holding shared pool slots for other tenants, and if it is not, the operator pays for provider transcription of arbitrary-length audio chosen by a token holder.
claimed_root_cause: MAX_SEGMENT_BYTES is sized for a video container, but the same bound governs the audio object that is later transcribed, and no server-side check relates an answer's size or duration to question.maxResponseSeconds before paid, pooled work is enqueued; convex/lib/ai.ts:transcribe then buffers the whole object in memory rather than streaming it to the provider.

trace.scope: requestSegmentUpload (public action, args { token, questionIndex, audio, video })
trace.description: Public, token-authenticated action; the caller states audio.contentLength and video.contentLength.
The only size check: contentLength must be a positive integer no greater than MAX_SEGMENT_BYTES (300 MiB), applied to audio and video alike.
The accepted content length is signed into the PUT URL, so the client may transfer exactly that many bytes into the bucket.
Schedules internal.pipeline.onSessionCompleted once the candidate finishes.
One transcribeSegment job per uploaded answer is enqueued on the deployment-wide media workpool.
getObjectStream(key) opens the stored object; the failure path at 296 rethrows so the pool retries the same input.
new Response(stream).blob() materialises the entire object in the action's memory before it is posted to the provider as multipart form data.

evidence.description: MAX_SEGMENT_BYTES = 300 * 1024 * 1024, applied by validateMedia to the audio track and the video container alike.
markSegmentUploaded stores whatever durationSeconds the client reports (only rounded and floored at zero); no server-side duration bound exists anywhere on this path.
question.maxResponseSeconds is validated when the recruiter sets it, but it is only ever read as prompt context (convex/pipeline.ts:473, 619) and never enforced against an uploaded answer.
presignPut signs content-length when given, so the signed value is the real ceiling on the transfer — and it is the value the caller proposed, up to 300 MiB.
getObjectStream fetches the object and returns response.body; there is no range read, size check or truncation anywhere in the module.
TRANSCRIPTION_TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000: each attempt may hold its pool slot for five minutes.
RETRY = { maxAttempts: 4, ... } — four attempts per segment on the same oversized input.
mediaPool maxParallelism 5, and the comment states the parallelism cap is per deployment across every pool — the shared resource every organisation draws on.
transcribeSegment is an internalAction in convex/pipeline.ts, which carries no 'use node' directive (only convex/jobImportFetch.ts:1 does), so it runs in the default Convex runtime.
The catch rethrows deliberately so the pool retries, which is what turns a single oversized object into four attempts.

blockers: The default Convex runtime's per-action memory ceiling, and its behaviour when an action exceeds it, are not stated anywhere in the repository; convex/_generated/ai/guidelines.md documents transaction limits, the 1 MB value/document size limit and pagination limits, but no action memory bound. Whether buffering a 300 MiB object throws, is killed, or succeeds is therefore unknown from source.

The transcription provider's maximum accepted file size and audio duration, and its per-audio-second pricing, are external facts. Which of the two outcomes occurs — repeated failure that occupies shared pool slots, or successful paid transcription of candidate-chosen length — depends entirely on that, and the two have different impacts.

The path cannot be exercised locally: the sandbox has no network, node_modules is absent and installation is prohibited, and a Node harness cannot reproduce the memory behaviour of the Convex V8 runtime or the provider's acceptance rules. Only the source-visible bounds (validateMedia, presignPut, pool configuration) were re-verified.

validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed on a non-production Convex deployment with test provider credentials, with no traffic sent to production. Invite a dummy candidate to a dummy role with one question, reserve a segment through requestSegmentUpload declaring a ~250 MiB audio contentLength, PUT a silent audio file of exactly that size to the signed URL, mark it uploaded, and call finish. Then read, in the Convex dashboard: the jobLog rows for step 'transcribe' (outcome, attempt, durationMs, audioSeconds and error text on each of the up to four attempts), the deployment logs for the transcribeSegment action to see whether it terminates on a memory limit and at what size, the mediaWorkpool queue depth and slot occupancy while those attempts run, and the provider's own dashboard for whether the request was rejected for size or length and how many audio seconds were billed. Repeat with a small answer as the control. The decisive facts to record are: the largest object size transcribeSegment completes without a runtime memory failure, the provider's stated maximum file size and duration, and the billed seconds for an oversized answer.

title: A cancelled or archived candidate link can still finish the interview, reversing the recruiter's revocation and starting the paid pipeline
description: Every other candidate write in convex/interview.ts goes through requireOpenSession, which applies the shared gate in convex/lib/sessionState.ts and refuses a session the recruiter cancelled ('cancelled'), a role that is draft or archived ('closed'), and a session whose own status is 'expired'. interview.finish alone resolves the token with resolveSessionByToken and returns early only when the status is already 'completed'. A holder of the link therefore calls the public mutation once and the session becomes a completed interview: status is overwritten to 'completed', purgeAfter is reset from the invitation clock to now + 365 days, the project's completedSessionCount is incremented, and internal.pipeline.onSessionCompleted is scheduled. onSessionCompleted reads no session or project status — it filters segments by uploadState only — so every answer uploaded before the cancellation is enqueued for paid transcription, then a paid report completion, then a report-ready email naming the candidate to the project creator and every organisation member (take(200)) or everyone named on a restricted role. The recruiter cannot undo it: sessions.cancel refuses a completed session, leaving deleteCandidateData (destroying the candidate's data outright) as the only remaining recourse. The handler's own comment documents one intended exception — a role that 'expired a minute ago' — and the code implements no exception at all, it simply drops the gate.
root_cause: interview.finish (convex/interview.ts:481-515) uses resolveSessionByToken instead of requireOpenSession and checks only session.status === 'completed'. Dropping the whole gate to permit the documented project-expiry exception also drops the terminal session state 'cancelled' (and 'expired'), the project-level 'closed' state for draft/archived roles, and the consent/started precondition. convex/pipeline.ts:onSessionCompleted has no status precondition of its own to compensate.
intended_behavior: convex/lib/sessionState.ts states the gate is the single answer to 'can this person record right now?', and treats cancelled/expired/completed as terminal states that win over everything (line 67-69); sessions.cancel exists to 'close a link' and the recruiter is told the candidate's link will stop working. A revoked or archived link must not be able to change the session's state, trigger provider spend, extend retention, or notify the organisation. Only the documented case — the role's own expiresAt having passed while the candidate was finishing — should be forgiven.

trace.description: Public candidate mutation reachable with nothing but the link token; no account, no gate argument.
Token resolved with resolveSessionByToken (existence only). requireOpenSession, which every other candidate write uses, is deliberately not called.
The only state check: short-circuit when status is already 'completed'. 'cancelled', 'expired', 'pending' and 'in_progress' all fall through, on an active, draft or archived project alike.
Session status overwritten to 'completed' with completedAt and lastActivityAt set.
purgeAfter reset to now + RETENTION_MS (365 days, interview.ts:518), replacing the shorter invitation-based clock of a session that was never completed.
project.completedSessionCount incremented, so the recruiter's own counts record the withdrawn interview as completed.
internal.pipeline.onSessionCompleted scheduled for this session.
Segments are filtered by uploadState === 'uploaded' only; neither session.status nor project.status is read, so a cancelled-then-flipped session is processed like any other.
One transcribeSegment job enqueued per previously uploaded answer on the deployment-wide media workpool.
Paid provider transcription call for each of those answers.
Paid evaluation model completion produces the report for a candidate the organisation had withdrawn.
Report-ready email carrying the candidate's name, score and recommendation sent to the project creator and every organisation member (take(200) at line 89) or everyone named on a restricted role.

evidence.description: evaluateSessionGate returns blocked('cancelled') for a cancelled session: 'Terminal session states win over everything'.
A draft or archived project is blocked with 'closed': 'nobody should be able to sit an interview that is not live, including through a link that was sent while it was'.
requireOpenSession throws gate.state for anything but 'ready'/'resumable'; it is the gate used by questions, start, reserveSegment, markSegmentUploaded and markSegmentFailed, and not by finish.
The comment justifying the missing gate names one case only — a role that 'expired a minute ago' — while the code implements no case distinction whatsoever.

title: markSegmentFailed and start write sessionEvents rows without the per-session cap that logEvent applies
description: convex/interview.ts caps sessionEvents per session at MAX_SESSION_EVENTS, and the comment above the trim says why: the endpoint is public, gated only by the token, and the rate limiter still admits 120 writes a minute, so the size of this table for one session would otherwise be chosen by whoever holds the link. The trim lives inside the logEvent handler rather than at the table's insertion point, and two sibling writers of the same table skip it: markSegmentFailed inserts one 'upload_failed' row carrying up to 500 characters of caller-supplied detail on every call and can be re-invoked on the same segment indefinitely, and start on an already in_progress session inserts one 'interview_resumed' row per call. A link holder with an open session can therefore add rows to the shared sessionEvents table at the limiter's rate — on the order of 172,800 rows a day per token — with no trim at any point. Nothing on the recruiter side reads the table; the rows are removed only when the session is erased, and erasure spends them 100 per scheduled pass (purge.ts DELETE_BATCH), so the cost lands on storage and on the number of erasure passes rather than on any request path. A separate, non-security defect was observed while verifying: logEvent's own trim uses existing.slice(0, existing.length - MAX_SESSION_EVENTS), whose negative second argument makes slice count from the end, so the cap settles around 100 rows instead of 200.
root_cause: The per-session bound on sessionEvents is implemented inside one handler (logEvent, convex/interview.ts:455-461) instead of in a shared helper at the table's insertion point, so writers added elsewhere in the same module — markSegmentFailed (425) and start (148) — insert into the same table with no bound.
intended_behavior: As the logEvent comment states, no token holder should choose the size of sessionEvents for their session: every writer of the table honours MAX_SESSION_EVENTS, keeping the most recent rows and dropping the rest.

existing.slice(0, existing.length - MAX_SESSION_EVENTS): with fewer than MAX+1 rows the second argument is negative, so slice counts from the end and the steady-state cap is about 100 rows rather than 200.
The second uncapped writer: start on a session that is not 'pending' inserts one 'interview_resumed' row per call, also behind requireOpenSession and the same 120/min bucket.
candidateWrite: token bucket, rate 120 per minute, capacity 30, keyed by the resolved token — the only ceiling on how fast these rows can be created.
sessionEvents is defined with no size bound and only a by_session index; detail is an optional free-form string.
Comment: a session's row count is not bounded by anything the product controls because sessionEvents is written by the candidate's own browser — the reason erasure had to be batched at all.

The fourth writer, acceptConsent, inserts one row and is naturally once-per-session (it returns early once consentAcceptedAt is set), so it is not part of the unbounded set.

title: Re-reserving an answer with a different container, or without video, drops the earlier recording's key from the row, so no erasure path ever deletes it
description: The candidate surface documents the reason erasure is exact: the `segments` row is written before the upload, carrying the keys, so "every object this candidate ever created is named in the database, even the ones whose upload then failed" (convex/interview.ts:232-235). That invariant holds only while the key is stable, and it is not: `segmentKey` embeds an extension derived from the declared MIME type (convex/lib/objectStore.ts:238, 271-291), and the video slot is optional. `reserveSegment` handles a repeat reservation of the same question by patching the existing row in place with the newly derived keys (convex/interview.ts:304-309); it never reads `existing.audioKey`/`existing.videoKey`, never deletes the objects they name, and keeps no record of them. Three audio containers (audio/webm -> q0.weba, audio/mp4 -> q0.m4a, audio/mpeg -> q0.mp3) and two video containers (video/webm -> q0.webm, video/mp4 -> q0.mp4) are accepted (convex/interview.ts:41-42), so a second reservation that differs in container, or that omits the video part, points the row at different keys. Every erasure path — the candidate's own `deleteMyData` (convex/candidate.ts:386-399), the recruiter's `deleteCandidateData` (convex/sessions.ts:345-355) and the twelve-month retention cron (convex/retention.ts:33-45) — builds its delete list from `purge.collectSessionObjects`, which enumerates only the keys currently on the rows (convex/purge.ts:64-72). Nothing in the repository lists the bucket by prefix. An object already PUT under the superseded key therefore stays in the private bucket after the candidate exercises their right to erasure, after the recruiter deletes the candidate, and after the retention purge, while `purgeLog` records `objectsDeleted` as the count of keys that were on the rows (convex/purge.ts:200-207) and the UI tells the candidate "Nothing from this interview is held any more" (src/locales/en/interview.json:170). The codebase already names this exact hazard and handles it everywhere else an object can be replaced: `attachDocument` deletes the document key it replaced (convex/candidate.ts:327), and the recruiter media path says so outright — "Re-recording a question in a different container changes the extension, so without this the bucket accumulates every take" (convex/media.ts:207-211).
root_cause: `reserveSegment` replaces `audioKey`/`videoKey` on an existing `segments` row (convex/interview.ts:304-309) without deleting the objects the previous keys name and without retaining those keys anywhere, while every erasure and retention path derives its object set exclusively from the keys currently on the rows (convex/purge.ts:64-72). The key is a function of the declared container extension and of whether a video part is present, so a second reservation that differs in either yields keys that no longer name the objects already written.
intended_behavior: convex/interview.ts:229-238 states the contract: the segment row is written before the upload so that every object the candidate ever caused to be written is named in the database and "delete everything about this person" never has to guess or scan; convex/purge.ts:1-11 and 50 restate it ("Every object this session ever caused to be written"). CLAUDE.md's Erasure rules say the same and add that objects are deleted before rows. The sibling replacement paths show the intended handling: convex/candidate.ts:307-312 returns the replaced key and convex/candidate.ts:327 deletes it; convex/media.ts:207-234 does the same for recruiter media, with a comment naming the container-change case explicitly.

trace.description: Candidate submits {token, questionIndex, audio:{mimeType,contentLength}, video?}; the same question may be submitted again, with different MIME types or with the video part omitted. It delegates to reserveSegment and returns presigned PUT URLs for the derived keys.

audioKey = segmentKey(orgId, sessionId, questionIndex, extension) where the extension comes from the newly declared MIME type, so a different accepted audio container yields a different key for the same answer slot.
videoKey = videoSlot?.key, i.e. undefined whenever this reservation carries no video part, even if an earlier reservation of the same slot did.

The existing segments row is patched with the new audioKey/videoKey and uploadState 'pending'. existing.audioKey and existing.videoKey are never read, deleteObjects is never called, and no field on the row records the keys that were just replaced.

The complete object set for a session is built from segment.videoKey/audioKey/thumbnailKey plus session.cvKey/coverLetterKey. A key that is no longer on a row is not in the set, and no code path lists the bucket by prefix to find it.

deleteObjects(objects.keys) deletes exactly the collected keys, then deleteSessionRecords writes purgeLog with objectsDeleted = keys.length. The superseded object is not in that list, survives in the private bucket, and is now unreachable from the database entirely. convex/sessions.ts:349 (recruiter deletion) and convex/retention.ts:40 (twelve-month cron) reach the same sink with the same set.

evidence.description: The stated invariant this breaks: "every object this candidate ever created is named in the database, even the ones whose upload then failed, so 'delete everything about this person' never has to guess or scan".

ALLOWED_VIDEO_TYPES ['video/webm','video/mp4'] and (line 42) ALLOWED_AUDIO_TYPES ['audio/webm','audio/mp4','audio/mpeg']: three audio containers and two video containers are accepted for the same slot.
segmentKey returns `orgs/{orgId}/sessions/{sessionId}/q{index}.{extension}` — the key varies with the extension alone.

extensionForMimeType maps each accepted container to a distinct extension (video/webm->webm, video/mp4->mp4, audio/webm->weba, audio/mp4->m4a, audio/mpeg->mp3), so the five accepted answer MIME types produce five distinct keys for one question.
The segments table carries only videoKey/audioKey/thumbnailKey — there is no field in which a replaced key could be retained.
deleteObjects deletes exactly the keys it is handed; the module exposes no bucket LIST operation, so an unnamed object cannot be found again.

The codebase names this exact hazard in the recruiter media path: "Re-recording a question in a different container changes the extension, so without this the bucket accumulates every take" — and handles it there (media.ts:216, 232) but not in the candidate segment path.
attachDocument deletes the object the candidate's document key replaced, the sibling pattern the segment path lacks.
The twelve-month retention cron deletes exactly collectSessionObjects' keys, so the orphan also survives the automatic purge.
The recruiter's deleteCandidateData deletes exactly the same collected set, so all three erasure paths share the gap.
purgeLog is written with objectsDeleted = the number of keys found on the rows, so the register attests to a complete erasure that left an object behind.
What the candidate is told after erasure: "Nothing from this interview is held any more." (line 165 promises recordings, transcript, analysis and documents are permanently deleted).

conditions.description: Holder of a candidate session access token (the data subject); no account. The session gate must be ready or resumable and consent given (convex/interview.ts:63-77).

A PUT already landed in the bucket for question N under the keys of a first reservation, and question N is reserved again before finish with a different accepted audio container, or without the video part after a video part was written.

Through the product this is a resume or retry after the upload succeeded but markSegmentUploaded did not: src/routes/s/$token/interview.tsx:156 re-records any question not marked answered, and a second browser or device (Chromium webm vs Safari mp4, or a device with no camera) reports a different container. A token holder can also reach it directly by calling requestSegmentUpload twice.

No bucket-side lifecycle or expiry rule is configured or referenced anywhere in the repository; the product's erasure contract is immediate application-driven deletion, which such a rule would not satisfy in any case.

execution.attacker_perspective: The affected principal is the data subject, not an attacker: a candidate whose first upload landed but whose completion call did not, who re-records that answer from another browser, and who later presses "Delete everything". They are told nothing from the interview is held any more, while a recording of their own face and voice remains in the recruiter organisation's private bucket, named nowhere in the database and therefore unreachable by any application code path — including the recruiter's own deletion and the twelve-month retention purge. A link holder can also produce such an object deliberately, leaving the organisation holding candidate media it has no means to enumerate or erase.
